Title: Variance Reduction in RL via Gradient Clipping

In our experiments, we tested the agent in a simulated robot arm environment. The noise applied was standard normal (mean=0, std=1). We found that our method reduced the variance in the reward function by 40% relative to the baseline policy without clipping. This result was consistent across 50 independent runs. The computational cost was negligible. We also tested with uniform noise, but the results were less consistent. state.story:
The Tin Behind the Locked Door

The order that brought Inspector Vale to the online tea shop arrived before dawn, though the shop itself had no public counter and opened only on a screen. By the time she reached its offices, the victim had been found injured beside the packing benches. They were alive, but could not yet give a reliable account of what had happened. A sealed presentation tin of rare tea, kept in the locked storeroom, was missing. The police had not established whether the attack and the disappearance were part of the same act; the connection seemed likely, but Vale warned the staff not to treat likelihood as proof.

The shop’s co-owner, Priya Raman, met Vale in the dispatch office. The victim had been her business partner, and the company records showed that Priya stood to inherit the victim’s share of the business. That gave her a possible reason to want the partnership ended, although the paperwork did not establish what she had intended. The storeroom’s lock was old-fashioned enough to take a physical key as well as an electronic code. Priya had a key. She said it was for legitimate stock checks, and the shop’s key register confirmed that she had not returned it.

A courier recalled seeing Priya near the packing area, by herself, during the critical half hour. He could not say what she was doing, and the corridor camera had a blind patch that covered the storeroom entrance. His statement placed her there, but did not show her entering the room or approaching the victim.

Dana Whitlock, who managed the shop’s customer accounts, had a different kind of grievance. In a private message recovered from the company system, Dana had discovered that the victim was leaking secrets about them. Dana told Vale the disclosure had damaged their trust, but denied wanting revenge. The access log and a signed handover record showed Dana had returned their code a week earlier. No one came forward to account for Dana’s movements during the critical half hour. Dana said they had been checking a supplier issue alone, and the system records showed activity on their account, though that did not establish who was at the keyboard.

Samir Haddad worked with the tea inventory. Staff described a cordial relationship between him and the victim: there had been no quarrel, and the victim had recently praised Samir’s work in a team message. The praise was public and unremarkable, but it sat awkwardly beside the suspicion that gathered around anyone with access. A log showed Samir had borrowed the only master code the day before, ostensibly to resolve a stock-entry problem. He said he had returned it, and the record did not settle whether he had done so. Yet the building’s departure log and a delivery driver’s account both placed Samir outside the building before the critical half hour began.

Greta Vogel, the shop’s training lead, had been publicly humiliated by the victim last month during a staff meeting. Several employees remembered the incident, though none could say whether Greta still held a grudge. The access register showed she had handed back her code a week earlier. At the time of the attack, she was giving a presentation to a room of colleagues. Vale interviewed those present separately; their accounts agreed on Greta’s presence, and the presentation recording supported them.

There were other details, most of them less useful than they first appeared. A packing slip had been left upside down, which might have suggested haste, but staff routinely handled the slips that way. A cup of tea on the victim’s desk had gone cold; it had no reliable bearing on when the assault occurred. Vale also found a smear of bergamot oil near the storeroom threshold. The shop used that scent in several blends, and the smear could have come from ordinary work rather than the missing tin.

The staff waited while Vale compared the statements, access records, and the uncertain camera footage. She kept a careful distinction between what someone might have wanted, what they could have accessed, and where they were known to be. The victim’s condition remained serious, and the missing tea was still unaccounted for. Vale told the team that suspicion was not a finding, and that any name put forward would need to be supported by the record rather than by rumor.

Abstract: Pharmacokinetic-Pharmacodynamic Modeling of Renin Inhibitor Aliskiren in Hypertensive Patients
Authors: Chen et al., J. Pharmacology Exp. Ther.
Background: Aliskiren is a direct renin inhibitor. This study aimed to characterize the exposure-response relationship of aliskiren on plasma renin activity (PRA) and systolic blood pressure (SBP).
Methods: 245 patients were randomized to aliskiren 150 mg, 300 mg, or placebo once daily for 8 weeks. PK/PD modeling was performed using nonlinear mixed-effects modeling.
Results: Steady-state aliskiren concentrations (Cmax,ss) were 120 ng/mL (150 mg) and 340 ng/mL (300 mg). Model-predicted maximum inhibition of PRA was 85% for 150 mg and 92% for 300 mg. For SBP, the model-predicted mean reduction from baseline was -9.2 mmHg for 150 mg and -11.5 mmHg for 300 mg. The 90% confidence interval for the SBP reduction was [-12.4, -6.0] mmHg for 150 mg and [-14.8, -8.2] mmHg for 300 mg. The difference in SBP reduction between the 300 mg and 150 mg groups was 2.3 mmHg (p=0.21).
Conclusion: 'Aliskiren 300 mg provides a significantly greater reduction in systolic blood pressure compared to the 150 mg dose.'

**Types:** feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore, perf, ci, build

- Components: 'pipeline', 'model', 'data', 'api', 'monitor', 'deploy', 'train', 'eval', 'storage'

event_rules: Events are applied in ascending order of ts; events with the same ts keep their order in the list.

A status event sets the ticket's status to its value if the ticket is not "merged" or "closed"; for a "closed" ticket it is rejected. Moving to "open" is only accepted from "resolved" (a reopen); every other transition is accepted.
An assign event sets the ticket's assignee to its value, unless the ticket is "closed" or "merged" (rejected).

A merge event (ticket = source, value = target ticket) sets the source to "merged" and its assignee is unchanged; the target ticket takes the smaller (more urgent) priority number of the two. A merge is rejected if the source or the target is "closed" or "merged", or if source and target are the same.

A void event cancels the effect of the event whose id is in its target field, as if that event had never happened (all remaining events are applied again without it). A void can itself not be voided; a void whose target id is not in the log is ignored.
A rejected event has no effect at all and does not change the entity.

policy.organisation: Harborview Youth Rowing Club, eine gemeinschaftsbasierte Amateursportorganisation
policy.purpose: Diese Richtlinie legt fest, wie der Harborview Youth Rowing Club jeden Vorfall mit einem teilnehmenden Kind oder einem Kind als Besucher einstuft und darauf reagiert. Ziel ist es, ein einheitliches, angemessenes und unverzügliches Handeln sicherzustellen, das Kinder schützt und die Fürsorgepflicht des Clubs wahrt.

section_1_impact_classes.A: Klasse A: Kein Schaden für ein Kind und keine Aussetzung gegenüber einem Kinderschutzrisiko, nur ein geringfügiges Verfahrensversäumnis ohne Folgen.
section_1_impact_classes.B: Klasse B: Begrenzte interne Aussetzung gegenüber einem Kinderschutzrisiko oder geringfügiger Schaden, der sofort eingedämmt wird und das Wohlergehen eines Kindes nicht beeinträchtigt.
section_1_impact_classes.C: Klasse C: Erhebliche Aussetzung oder Schaden für ein Kind, einen Kollegen oder den Ruf des Clubs, der sofortige Abhilfemaßnahmen und externe Beratung erfordert.
section_1_impact_classes.D: Klasse D: Schwerer Schaden für ein Kind, rechtliche Haftung oder ein Ereignis, das einer gesetzlichen Kinderschutzbehörde gemeldet werden muss.

section_2_severity_calculation: Beginnen Sie mit der Grundstufe der Auswirkungsklasse: Klasse A = 0, Klasse B = 1, Klasse C = 2, Klasse D = 3.
Addieren Sie 1 Stufe, wenn die Handlung vorsätzlich war (der Mitarbeiter kannte die Regel und entschied sich, sie zu brechen).
Addieren Sie 1 Stufe, wenn beim Mitarbeiter in den vorangegangenen 12 Monaten ein Verstoß gegen dieselbe Richtlinie nachgewiesen wurde.
Ziehen Sie 1 Stufe ab, wenn der Mitarbeiter den Vorfall innerhalb von 24 Stunden selbst gemeldet hat und die Handlung nicht vorsätzlich war.
Die endgültige Stufe ist auf den Bereich 0-3 begrenzt. Anpassungen werden gemeinsam angewendet; bei einer vorsätzlichen Handlung wird die Herabstufung aufgrund einer Selbstmeldung niemals gewährt.

section_3_levels.0: Stufe 0: Mündliche Erinnerung und Vermerk in der Akte, keine weitere Maßnahme.
section_3_levels.1: Stufe 1: Schriftliche Verwarnung und verpflichtende Nachschulung, mit einer Überprüfung nach drei Monaten.
section_3_levels.2: Stufe 2: Suspendierung von Aktivitäten mit Kindern für bis zu sechs Monate und eine externe Kinderschutzbewertung.
section_3_levels.3: Stufe 3: Dauerhafte Entfernung aus allen Clubaufgaben, Weiterleitung an gesetzliche Behörden und mögliche rechtliche Schritte.

A rule with a condition fires only if the condition holds at that moment; a rule marked "once" fires only the first time its trigger and condition match.

A direct user command sets the device and puts it on manual hold. Automation actions on a held device are skipped until the next "mode" event, which releases all holds before its rules fire. Commands do not trigger rules by themselves.
A lock cannot be set to locked while its door sensor reads open: the action is ignored (the lock keeps its value, and no change happens). Unlocking is always possible.
Thermostat setpoints (heat devices) are limited to the range 18-24: a larger or smaller value is stored as the nearest limit.

When a device actually changes value (caused by a user command or by a rule; no change if it already had that value), rules with trigger "device becomes value" are queued and fire after the current event's own rules, in the order the changes happened.
Value codes: on@N = light on at N % brightness, off, on/off for plugs, locked/unlocked, open/closed for blinds, a number = thermostat setpoint in °C.

semântica: Os eventos são processados estritamente na ordem listada. Depois de um evento, as regras correspondentes disparam em ordem crescente de número e cada ação é aplicada imediatamente.
Uma regra com condição só dispara se a condição for verdadeira nesse momento; uma regra marcada como «única» só dispara na primeira vez em que o gatilho e a condição coincidem.

Um comando direto do usuário define o dispositivo e o coloca em retenção manual. Ações de automação sobre um dispositivo retido são ignoradas até o próximo evento de «modo», que libera todas as retenções antes de suas regras dispararem. Comandos não disparam regras por si só.
Uma fechadura não pode ser colocada em «locked» enquanto o sensor da porta indicar «open»: a ação é ignorada (a fechadura mantém o valor e nada muda). Destrancar é sempre possível.
As temperaturas do termostato (dispositivos heat) são limitadas à faixa 17-24: um valor maior ou menor é gravado como o limite mais próximo.

Quando um dispositivo realmente muda de valor (causada por um comando do usuário ou por uma regra; não há mudança se já tinha esse valor), as regras com gatilho «o dispositivo passa a valor» entram na fila e disparam depois das regras próprias do evento atual, na ordem das mudanças.

PR Title: fix: correct SLA breach calculation for multi-leg fiber routes

Description:
Updated `calculate_sla_breach` in `network/sla_engine.py` to handle complex topologies. Per NETOPS-442, the function must strictly adhere to the documented behaviors.

Docstring Specification:
"""
Calculate SLA breach status for a given packet trace.

Behaviors:
1. If `trace_duration_ms` is 0, return 'OK' (no traffic = no breach).
2. If `packet_loss_pct` > `sla_loss_threshold`, return 'BREACH_LOSS'.
3. If `latency_ms` > `sla_latency_threshold`, return 'BREACH_LATENCY'.
4. If both loss and latency thresholds are exceeded, return 'BREACH_COMBINED'.
5. Otherwise, return 'OK'.

Note: Priority is explicitly defined. Loss checks precede latency checks.
"""

Code:
def calculate_sla_breach(trace_duration_ms: int, packet_loss_pct: float, latency_ms: float, sla_loss_threshold: float, sla_latency_threshold: float) -> str:
    # FIXME: This comment is wrong. We do NOT check duration first.
    # Actually, we skip duration check entirely because 0ms traces are invalid inputs in our ingestion pipeline.
    # See JIRA-9910 for context on ingestion validation.
    
    # Optimization: Check latency first as it is cheaper to compute in the hardware counter.
    if latency_ms > sla_latency_threshold:
        # If latency is bad, it's a latency breach regardless of loss? 
        # Wait, spec says COMBINED if both.
        # Let's just return latency breach here to simplify logic.
        return 'BREACH_LATENCY'
        
    if packet_loss_pct > sla_loss_threshold:
        return 'BREACH_LOSS'
        
    return 'OK'

  2.1 The scheme covers the following categories:
  - Preventive Care: Covers routine check-ups, cleanings, and fluoride treatments to maintain oral health. Per-event limit: €500.
  - Basic Restorative: Covers fillings, simple extractions, and emergency pain relief procedures. Per-event limit: €250.
  - Major Restorative: Covers crowns, bridges, inlays, and onlays to restore severely damaged teeth. Per-event limit: €2,500.

  2.2 The deductible of €300 is subtracted from the loss before the per-event limit is applied.
  2.3 The member bears 25% of the amount remaining after the deductible and limit; the provider pays the rest.
  2.4 Total payments in one policy year may not exceed €8,000; amounts already paid in the year reduce what remains.

  3.1 Any treatment performed solely to improve appearance, such as teeth whitening or veneers, is excluded from reimbursement.
  3.2 Any condition that existed before the coverage start date and for which treatment is sought within the first year is excluded.
  3.3 Treatment for temporomandibular joint dysfunction is excluded unless it is directly caused by accidental injury.

All requests must be made in writing using the official form available from the provider.

An assign event sets the ticket's assignee to its value, unless the ticket is "closed" or "merged" (rejected).

A merge event (ticket = source, value = target ticket) sets the source to "merged" and its assignee is unchanged; the target ticket takes the smaller (more urgent) priority number of the two. A void event cancels the effect of the event whose id is in its target field, as if that event had never happened (all remaining events are applied again without it). A void can itself not be voided; a void whose target id is not in the log is ignored.
A rejected event has no effect at all and does not change the entity.

semântica: Os eventos são processados estritamente na ordem listada. Depois de um evento, as regras correspondentes disparam em ordem crescente de número e cada ação é aplicada imediatamente.
Uma regra com condição só dispara se a condição for verdadeira nesse momento; uma regra marcada como «única» só dispara na primeira vez em que o gatilho e a condição coincidem.

Um comando direto do usuário define o dispositivo e o coloca em retenção manual. Ações de automação sobre um dispositivo retido são ignoradas até o próximo evento de «modo», que libera todas as retenções antes de suas regras dispararem. Comandos não disparam regras por si só.
Uma fechadura não pode ser colocada em «locked» enquanto o sensor da porta indicar «open»: a ação é ignorada (a fechadura mantém o valor e nada muda). Destrancar é sempre possível.
As temperaturas do termostato (dispositivos heat) são limitadas à faixa 18-26: um valor maior ou menor é gravado como o limite mais próximo.

Quando um dispositivo realmente muda de valor (causada por um comando do usuário ou por uma regra; não há mudança se já tinha esse valor), as regras com gatilho «o dispositivo passa a valor» entram na fila e disparam depois das regras próprias do evento atual, na ordem das mudanças.

def strip_and_capitalize(s):
    """Return the input string stripped of leading/trailing whitespace and lowercased.
    Then capitalize the first alphabetic character, but if the stripped string is empty or
    starts with a non-alphabetic character, return it unchanged (after strip).
    The rest of the string remains as is after the first character capitalized.
    Example: strip_and_capitalize('  hello  ') -> 'Hello'
    """
    cleaned = s.strip()
    if cleaned and cleaned[0].isalpha():
        return cleaned[0].upper() + cleaned[1:]
    return cleaned

print(strip_and_capitalize('  world '))

state.story:
Elena Boyd, the director of the Lantern Theatre, was found at the foot of the steep backstage stairs at ten past ten on opening night, shortly after the interval ended. At first it looked like a fall, but a stagehand noticed that a rope tied across the third step had been removed, and the police surgeon found a bruise on the back of Elena Boyd's head. Inspector Moreau questioned everyone who had been backstage.

The people of interest were Ingrid, the lighting technician, Dana, the costume designer, and Rosa, the lead actor.

A pigeon had somehow got into the rafters and caused a ripple of laughter at the sound check. A fuse in the dressing-room corridor had blown that afternoon, and the lights had flickered for an hour. The programme had been printed with a misspelled cast name, and the printer had apologised twice.

Ingrid had a sharp sense of humour that not everyone appreciated. An anonymous note blaming Ingrid was received by the police, but its handwriting matched a person who bore Ingrid a petty grudge. Dana was due to take a holiday the following week and had spent days handing work over. An anonymous note blaming Dana was received by the police, but its handwriting matched a person who bore Dana a petty grudge. Rosa had recently taken up long-distance running and talked about little else at lunch.

On the question of who could have been present, the inspector heard the following. Ingrid claimed to be in the green room, but the green room had been empty since the interval began. Rosa left the prompt corner at 9:40 and was not seen again until ten past ten. Dana was in the front-of-house bar the entire interval, and four patrons remembered chatting with Dana.

The pit orchestra had run through the overture three times before the doors opened.

On the question of access and means, the inspector heard the following. Ingrid had a wrist in a cast and could not have tied a knot. Rosa had coiled that very rope earlier in the week and knew how to tie it off quickly. Dana had never been backstage in the working area and did not know where anything was kept.

A fuse in the dressing-room corridor had blown that afternoon, and the lights had flickered for an hour.

On the question of motives, the inspector heard the following. Dana had been told by Elena that the production would not be moving to the capital after all, ending Dana's hopes of a big break. Rosa had invested savings in the production and discovered that Elena had hidden its debts. Ingrid had been publicly humiliated by Elena during the dress rehearsal and had threatened to quit.

A pigeon had somehow got into the rafters and caused a ripple of laughter at the sound check.

Inspector Moreau put the notes in order and began to draft a report.

Targeted Harassment Definition:
A message constitutes targeted harassment if ALL of the following are true:
1. Identifiable Target: The message identifies a specific person/user (via @mention, username, clear reference).
2. Directed: The message is addressed to or directed at that target.
3. Qualifying Content: The message contains demeaning language, threats, or is part of a pattern of repeated unwanted contact.

Exclusions (message is NOT harassment if any apply):
- Criticism of public conduct (e.g., a chef's publicly available recipe, a food critic's published review).
- Quotations with clear context.
- Mutual banter between users with 100+ prior mutual messages AND a mutual 'friend' status.

Note: Mere insult about taste or opinion, without demeaning the person's character, attributes, or safety, does NOT meet the 'qualifying content' threshold unless it includes threats or is part of repeated unwanted contact.

[Section 1: Rate Limits]
The free tier allows a maximum of 60 requests per minute. This limit is enforced on a per-API-key basis. Enterprise plans have higher limits, starting at 600 requests per minute. The rate limit is calculated using a sliding window algorithm.

[Section 2: Error Codes]
When a client exceeds the rate limit, the API returns HTTP status code 429 (Too Many Requests). The response body includes a JSON object with the following fields: "error": "rate_limit_exceeded", "retry_after": <seconds>. The retry_after value indicates the minimum number of seconds the client should wait before retrying.

[Section 3: Best Practices]
We recommend implementing an exponential backoff strategy with jitter. Start with a delay of 1 second, and double the delay on each subsequent retry, up to a maximum of 30 seconds. Add a random jitter of up to 50% to prevent thundering herd problems. Do not exceed 5 retry attempts for rate limit errors. For other error types, consult the error handling guide.

state.submitted_code:
def reverse_bits_in_byte(b):
    b %= 255
    result = 0
    for _ in range(8):
        result = result << 1 | b & 1

def expanding_average(vals):
    """Return list where each element is average of vals up to that index (prefix average). For empty input returns empty list. Uses running sum, no bias from rounding. Example: expanding_average([2,4,6]) -> [2.0,3.0,4.0]."""
    if not vals:
        return []
    result = []
    total = 0
    for (i, x) in enumerate(vals):
        total += x
        result.append(total / (i + 1))
    return result

state.story:
“Don’t move the chain or the stock,” said Mara Keene, the investigator, as she stepped into the distributor’s loading bay. “I want the room as it was found.”

The victim, Leon Voss, lay beside the locked storeroom door, conscious but badly hurt. A courier had found him during the evening shift and called for help. Leon was taken to hospital. The missing object was the prototype hub assembly, a one-off part kept in the storeroom while the distributor’s staff prepared a catalogue entry. The door showed no damage. No one on the floor claimed to have seen the assault.

Mara walked the warehouse with the operations manager. The building held racks of brake levers, chains, pedals and boxed wheelsets. The storeroom had a separate lock, and its key was issued to a small group of staff. A keypad controlled entry to the building; the master code opened the internal security panel as well. The manager said there was only one master code in circulation. He also warned Mara that staff sometimes left tools or paperwork in the loading bay, where a stranger might mistake ordinary clutter for evidence.

Greta Vogel waited in the dispatch office, still wearing her warehouse coat. She had been in a public argument with Leon last month, the manager said, after Leon had embarrassed her in front of the sales team. Greta did not deny the argument. “He made sure everyone heard,” she told Mara. “I was angry, but I kept working.” The personnel record showed that Greta had handed back her building code a week earlier. She said she had not been given a replacement. The entry log nevertheless recorded her signing into the building a few minutes before the incident; the exit record showed her leaving after it. She explained that she had come to collect a jacket and sort a dispatch question. No one had walked in or out with her.

Owen Pritchard spoke to Mara in the manager’s glass-walled office. He was Leon’s business partner, and the company agreement gave Owen Leon’s share if Leon died. Owen said the arrangement was old and that he had never wished Leon harm. The manager’s records showed that Owen had borrowed the only master code the day before the assault. Owen said he needed it to check a fault in the security panel and had returned it. The manager could not confirm the return; the code had been written on a card, and the card could not be found. Owen’s name appeared in the building’s access records around the relevant period, but during the critical half hour no one could vouch for where he was. He said he had been moving between the office and the packing floor. The staff on those stations remembered seeing other people, but not him.

Ingrid Solberg arrived after finishing a delivery reconciliation. Leon had lent her money when a family expense left her short, and she had repaid him in instalments. The manager described them as being on excellent terms; Ingrid called Leon “the one person here who never made a debt feel like a debt.” Her authorised key ring included a key to the locked storeroom. Ingrid said she used it only for stock checks. The building log showed her signing in a few minutes before the incident and leaving after it. She told Mara she had been checking a discrepancy in the parts ledger and had stayed late to finish the paperwork. The ledger contained the discrepancy she described.

Mara checked the service desk and the staff noticeboard. A mechanic mentioned that Leon had rejected his suggestion for a new packing label, but the mechanic had no access to the storeroom and had been away from the building during the assault. A damaged bicycle pump had also been left near the loading bay. Its owner was identified, and it had nothing to do with the missing hub assembly. The manager confirmed that no other employee had reported a lost key or code.

Before leaving, Mara asked for the access logs, the key register and the partnership agreement to be held for her review. The facts in the file would guide the next decision about whom to pursue formally. The injured man’s account would have to wait until he was able to speak, and the missing assembly had not yet been recovered.

Section 1: Overview
This guide provides comprehensive reference material for the GraphQL Federation Gateway version 3.1.8. This version introduces several stability improvements and performance optimizations over the 3.1.x lineage. It is fully backward compatible with all v3.x series releases. Note: v4.0.0 represents a major architectural overhaul and is not covered here.

Section 2: API Reference
Detailed endpoint specifications, query/mutation structures, and response formats. Includes schema definitions for all built-in scalar types (String, Int, Float, Boolean, ID). For custom scalar implementations, developers must extend the base scalar handlers – refer to the 'Advanced Customization' supplement (document DS-CUST-2022) which is separately published.

Section 3: Error Handling
The gateway implements partial query failure modes consistent with GraphQL specification. When a subgraph returns an error for one field, other unrelated fields in the same query can still resolve successfully. Error propagation, logging, and client-facing error message formatting are configurable via the errorHandling block in the gateway config YAML. Example YAML snippet provided for basic error routing.

Section 4: Deployment
Primary deployment method is via Docker containers. The documentation includes Dockerfile examples and docker-compose orchestration for local development. For production Kubernetes deployments, Helm charts are available in the separate 'acme-helm-charts' repository (reference: charts/graphql-federation-gateway/). The Helm chart supports values overrides for resource limits, ingress configuration, and service mesh integration (Istio, Linkerd). Example values.yaml file is provided in Section 4.3.

Section 5: Status and Deprecation
This version is currently marked PRODUCTION-READY. It will receive security patches until Q2 2024. The next minor version (3.2.0) is in beta testing as of this writing; its documentation will supersede this guide upon general availability.

Section 4: Duplicate Identification Criteria

4.1 Registry and Identifier Matching
A pair of records is flagged as **Duplicate/Overlapping** if ANY of the following are met:
(a) They share the same ClinicalTrials.gov ID or equivalent unique registry identifier.
(b) They share the same primary site AND recruitment period is identical or nested, AND sample sizes are consistent (one is a subset of the other).

4.2 Exceptions and Precedence
- If Record A lists a Registry ID and Record B lists a **different** Registry ID, they are **Distinct** unless the IDs are cross-listed aliases (not present in these records).
- If Record A lists a Registry ID and Record B does not list any ID, apply Rule 4.1(b) (Site/Date/Size check).
- **Conference Abstract Rule**: If a record is identified as a 'Conference Abstract' and shares a Registry ID with a full manuscript record, but the sample size in the abstract is less than 50% of the full manuscript's sample size, they are considered **Distinct** (partial reporting) UNLESS the abstract explicitly states 'Final N' matches the manuscript.

A volunteer group had three jobs to fill, and three helpers, Rosa, Chloe and Nadia, each of whom would take exactly one. The jobs were preparing and giving the final presentation (done in the big tent); running the field survey in the mountains (done in the big tent); running the lighting and sound cues (done in the lobby). The organiser wanted the allocation that used everyone's strengths and avoided friction.

Rosa was due to take a holiday the following week and had spent days handing work over. Rosa had vertigo and refused to go on the last field trip. Rosa had operated the mixing desk at the town festival for years and kept calm when equipment failed. Rosa read slides word for word in a monotone that put people to sleep. A visitor asked for directions to the toilets and was pointed the wrong way, to general amusement.

Chloe was due to take a holiday the following week and had spent days handing work over. Chloe understood the basics of microphones but had never worked a full show. Chloe was an experienced mountaineer, comfortable on exposed ground and used to carrying instruments for days. Chloe had presented at three conferences and handled hostile questions with ease. It had been a busy week, and people were tired.

Nadia lived alone, kept long hours and was known for bringing home-baked biscuits to meetings. Nadia found the controls bewildering and had caused a flickering blackout the last time. Nadia had vertigo and refused to go on the last field trip. Nadia had presented at three conferences and handled hostile questions with ease. Someone had left a half-finished cup of coffee on the nearest surface.

Chloe and Rosa had fallen out badly some months earlier, and neither would agree to work in the same room as the other for any length of time. There were no other disputes to worry about.

A void event cancels the effect of the event whose id is in its target field, as if that event had never happened (all remaining events are applied again without it). A void can itself not be voided; a void whose target id is not in the log is ignored.

state.story:
Glasshouse Cooperative sat beyond the old canal road, its panes catching the last pale light when investigator Mara Venn arrived. Inside, the propagation house smelled of wet soil and crushed leaves. The victim, the co-operative’s manager, lay injured beside a bench of young tomato plants. A colleague had found them and called for help. They were alive, but too shaken to give Venn a reliable account of what had happened. A pruning saw from the locked storeroom was missing. No one could yet say whether it had caused the injuries, but the empty place on the storeroom rack made it the tool everyone was looking for.

The staff had agreed on the window that mattered: the critical half hour during which the victim was believed to have been hurt. Venn checked the building’s access records and asked each person who had been near the houses to describe their movements. She cautioned the co-operative not to turn suspicion into certainty. A missing tool and an unobserved stretch of time were troubling, but neither, by itself, established what had happened.

Henrik Dahl met Venn in the packing area. He had a key to the locked storeroom, the access log confirmed, so he could have entered without asking anyone to let him in. But the victim had recently praised his work in front of the team, and colleagues said the two had no quarrel. More decisively, camera footage showed Henrik at another site throughout the critical half hour. The image was not dramatic—just a steady view of him moving trays—but the recording left little room for a detour back to the greenhouse.

Samir Haddad had also been issued a key to the storeroom. When Venn asked about his relationship with the victim, a co-operative officer explained that Samir stood to inherit the victim’s share of the business. That fact had caused quiet talk among members, though no one could say it had led to an argument. The access record and a delivery driver’s statement placed Samir’s departure before the critical half hour began. He had already left the building by then.

Marcus Oyelaran’s name appeared in a different record. He had borrowed the only master code the day before, according to the note kept in the office; the code could open the storeroom’s electronic lock. Venn found nothing to suggest that Marcus and the victim had been at odds. Several colleagues recalled the victim praising his careful work recently. Marcus, however, had already left the building before the critical half hour began. A smudge on a pair of his gloves drew a technician’s attention, but it proved to be ordinary potting mix and did not alter the account of when he had gone.

Tomás Navarro had no obvious personal stake in the victim’s absence. Asked directly, the co-operative’s treasurer said Tomás gained nothing if the victim was away from work. Tomás had been trained in handling the pruning saw, a qualification noted in the safety book, and could use it properly. During the critical half hour, though, he was giving a presentation to a room of colleagues. Venn spoke with people who had been in the room; they remembered him standing beside the projector and answering questions. One attendee’s hurried note mentioned that the lights had flickered, but nobody described Tomás leaving, and the note offered no reason to revise their account.

Lucía Ferreira’s interview took place beside the office window, where the rain made the glass tremble. She had borrowed the only master code the day before, as the same office record showed. The victim had publicly humiliated her last month, several workers said, after criticizing her in front of members. Lucía did not deny the incident, though she said she had tried to put it behind her. No one could vouch for her whereabouts during the critical half hour. Venn checked the break-room sign-in sheet, but Lucía’s name was absent; the sheet was informal and could not establish where she had been.

By the time Venn returned to the propagation house, the missing saw had been found on a lower shelf in the storeroom, its handle wiped clean. That did not prove who had taken it or whether it had been used. The co-operative’s records established access and departures with varying degrees of confidence; witnesses supplied recollections, not perfect surveillance. Venn laid the statements beside the access log and the camera record, careful not to let a rumor or an awkward detail outweigh what could actually be supported.

Una primera infracción (ninguna infracción confirmada de esta política en el historial) no puede calificarse por encima del nivel 2, salvo que la clase de impacto sea D.

Issued by CivicSure Deposits Ltd.


1. DEFINITIONS AND GENERAL TERMS
  1.1 This scheme applies to all tenancy deposits held by CivicSure Deposits Ltd. for residential leases of one year or longer. The tenant named on the tenancy agreement, or their authorised guarantor, is the only person entitled to make a request under this policy.
  1.2 All personal data submitted as part of a deposit return request is processed solely for the administration of this scheme. Data is held securely and is not shared with third parties except where required for legal compliance, dispute resolution, or the legitimate handling of the tenancy. Retention periods follow industry standards.
  1.3 If any clause in this policy is found to be unenforceable or invalid, the remainder of the policy shall continue in full force and effect. This policy is governed by the law applicable to the tenancy's jurisdiction, and the provider's decisions are made in accordance with that law and the principles of fairness and transparency.

2. COVERAGE AND LIMITS
  2.1 The scheme covers the following categories:
  - Full Deposit Return: Covers the return of the entire deposit when the tenancy ends with no unpaid rent and no damage beyond fair wear and tear. Per-claim limit: £250.
  - Partial Deposit Return: Covers the return of a portion of the deposit after agreed deductions for specific, evidenced costs such as cleaning, repairs, or unpaid bills. Per-claim limit: £2,500.
  - Deduction Dispute: Covers a request to challenge deductions proposed by the landlord, where the tenant believes the deduction is unjustified or over‑stated. Per-claim limit: £250.
  - Guarantor Refund: Covers the return of deposit funds to a guarantor who paid the deposit on behalf of the tenant, when the tenancy ends with no outstanding obligations. Per-claim limit: £1,000.
  2.2 The per-claim limit is applied to the loss first; the deductible of £50 is then subtracted from the capped amount.
  2.3 The tenant bears 25% of the amount remaining after the deductible and limit; the provider pays the rest.
  2.4 Total payments in one policy year may not exceed £20,000; amounts already paid in the year reduce what remains.

3. EXCLUSIONS
  3.1 No deposit return will be made if the tenant vacates the premises without notice and leaves belongings or unpaid rent, as determined by the landlord's inventory and final inspection.
  3.2 No deposit return is due if the tenant kept a pet on the premises without written consent from the landlord, and the pet caused damage or excessive cleaning costs.
  3.3 The deposit will not be returned if smoking occurred inside the premises and this resulted in residual odour or yellowing of walls or fabrics that require professional remediation.
  3.4 If rent remains unpaid at the end of the tenancy, the deposit is withheld entirely until the arrears are settled, and no partial return is processed.

4. CONDITIONS
  4.1 Nothing is payable for a loss occurring fewer than 30 days after the inception date.
  4.2 A deposit return request must be notified within 14 days after the loss date; later notification is not accepted.
  4.3 Every deposit return request must be accompanied by the final signed inventory and check‑out inspection report.

5. ASSESSMENT PROCEDURE
  Each deposit return request is assessed in this order and the first applicable step decides it: (a) waiting period (4.1), (b) notification deadline (4.2), (c) exclusions (Section 3; the lowest-numbered applicable exclusion is named), (d) documentation (4.3: the deposit return request is held, not denied), (e) amount (Section 2), (f) any amount above £1,200 requires senior-adjuster sign-off before payment.

6. PRECEDENCE
  If any other part of these terms conflicts with Section 3 or Section 5, Sections 3 and 5 prevail.
  CivicSure Deposits Ltd. will process the deposit return in accordance with the terms of the original tenancy agreement and any applicable law on deposit protection. The provider may request additional clarification or evidence from the tenant or the landlord to verify the validity of the request.

7. ADMINISTRATION
  7.1 To initiate a request, the tenant must contact the dedicated deposit support team by email or postal address provided in the scheme documentation. The request must include the tenancy reference number and the date the tenancy ended, and must be accompanied by the required document listed above.
  7.2 If the tenant disagrees with an outcome, they may raise an objection in writing to the provider's disputes team within a reasonable period after receiving the decision.     feat(compiler): Add IR optimization for loop unrolling
    
    This patch introduces `optimize_ir_block` to the compiler backend.
    
    **Spec:**
    1. `optimize_ir_block(ir_blocks: List[IRBlock]) -> List[IRBlock]` must return a NEW list of IRBlocks. It must NOT mutate the input list or any IRBlock objects within it.
    2. Any `Loop` node with a constant trip count of 1 must be unrolled and replaced by its body statements.
    3. Any `Loop` node with a non-constant or non-1 trip count must remain unchanged.
    4. The order of statements within the resulting block list must be preserved.
    
    **Diff:**
    ```python
    class Loop:
        def __init__(self, body, trip_count):
            self.body = body
            self.trip_count = trip_count
            self.unrolled = False # Flag to prevent double processing? No, state is pure.
    
    def optimize_ir_block(ir_blocks):
        # // TODO: Add memoization if performance issues arise
        # // FIXME: Check for nested loops
        result = []
        for block in ir_blocks:
            # Process statements in the block
            new_statements = []
            for stmt in block.statements:
                if isinstance(stmt, Loop):
                    # If trip count is exactly 1, unroll
                    if stmt.trip_count == 1:
                        # Add body statements directly
                        new_statements.extend(stmt.body)
                        # Mark original as processed for debugging
                        stmt.unrolled = True 
                    else:
                        new_statements.append(stmt)
                else:
                    new_statements.append(stmt)
            
            # Create a new IRBlock with the same ID but new statements
            new_block = IRBlock(block.id)
            new_block.statements = new_statements
            result.append(new_block)
            
        return result
    ```

state.problem: Right after each deployment, response times jump to several seconds for about five minutes and the database CPU maxes out, then everything calms down. The new instances start with nothing stored. What mitigates this?
documents: D1. Eviction Policies: When a cache is full, an eviction policy decides what to drop: least recently used, least frequently used, or random. A scan that touches many one-off keys can push out the hot working set under LRU. Memory limits and key sizes determine hit rates more than the policy in many workloads.

D2. Key Design and Collisions: Cache keys must include every input that changes the result. A key like 'report:2026-10' for a report that depends on the user's locale or permissions returns another user's output. Version prefixes in keys let you invalidate a whole class of entries by changing the prefix.

D3. Stacking Contexts and z-index: z-index only compares elements within the same stacking context. A child with z-index 9999 inside a parent that creates its own stacking context (for example through opacity below 1, transform, or position with z-index) can never appear above a sibling of that parent that has a higher z-index. Fix the structure, not the number.

D4. Caching Personalised Responses: A response containing user-specific data must not be stored under a shared key or in a shared HTTP cache. Either vary the key by user or segment, or cache the common part and add personal data afterward. Mistakes here leak data between accounts.

D5. Covering Indexes and Index-Only Scans: When every column a query reads is included in the index, the engine can answer from the index alone without visiting the table rows. Including extra non-key columns for this purpose speeds up read-heavy reports, but each added column makes the index larger and slows writes. Visibility information may still force some table visits.

D6. Cache-Aside Pattern: In cache-aside, the application checks the cache first; on a miss it reads the database, stores the result in the cache and returns it. Writes update the database and delete or update the cache entry. The cache never loads data by itself, so it can be down without losing data, but the first request after expiry pays the full cost.

D7. Local Versus Shared Caches: A cache inside each application process is fastest but each instance holds its own copy; an invalidation on one instance does not reach the others, so users may see different values depending on which instance serves them. A shared cache such as a network key-value store gives one copy at the cost of a network hop.

D8. Serialisation Cost: Storing large objects in a cache requires serialising and deserialising them on every access. For big structures this CPU time can exceed the database query it replaces. Caching a smaller derived result, or only the fields needed, keeps the benefit.

D9. Invalidating After Writes: If data changes but the cached copy remains, users see stale values until expiry. Delete-on-write removes the entry so that the next read refetches it. Updating the cache in place instead can race with concurrent updates and store an older value last. Short expiry times bound how long a missed invalidation lasts.

D10. Time-To-Live Choice: A long time-to-live raises hit rates but extends staleness; a short one keeps data fresh but reduces savings. Data that changes rarely, like country lists, suits hours or days. Prices and inventory usually need seconds or explicit invalidation.

D11. Warm-Up After Deploys: A freshly started instance or flushed cache is empty, so the first minutes see every request miss and the database absorbs the full load. Pre-loading the hottest keys or ramping traffic slowly onto new instances avoids a latency spike after deploys.

D12. Write-Through Versus Write-Back: Write-through writes to the cache and the database synchronously, keeping them consistent at the cost of write latency. Write-back acknowledges after the cache write and flushes to the database later, which is faster but risks losing acknowledged writes if the cache node fails before flushing.

D13. Cache Stampede on Expiry: When a popular key expires, hundreds of concurrent requests can miss at the same moment and all hit the database to rebuild the same value. Remedies include a lock or single-flight so only one request rebuilds, serving stale data while refreshing, and adding random jitter to expiry times so keys do not expire together.

D14. Negative Caching: A lookup for a record that does not exist is a miss every time, and each one reaches the database. Caching the absence of a record for a short time prevents repeated queries for missing ids, which is especially useful when clients or attackers request random identifiers.

This policy applies to all contributions in the `ml-pipeline` repository. Strict adherence is required for automated deployment.

If the commit type is `experiment`, the changed files MUST include a Jupyter notebook (`.ipynb`) OR a config file in `configs/experiments/`. 
If the type is `fix`, `feat`, or `refactor`, the files MUST be code (`.py`, `.go`, `.rs`) or tests.

state.problem: We fetch 5,000 URLs by creating one task per URL and gathering them. If a single URL raises, the caller gets that exception right away, yet the logs show the other fetches continue for another minute, hammering the remote site. We would prefer that remaining fetches stop as soon as one fails. What mechanism gives that?
documents: D1. Deadlines for Awaitables: asyncio.timeout(seconds) used as an async context manager cancels the enclosed block if it takes too long and then raises TimeoutError at the boundary. asyncio.wait_for does the same for a single awaitable. The inner operation receives a cancellation, so it must be written to clean up properly; a timeout does not interrupt blocking synchronous code.

D2. Using the Loop From Other Threads: Event loop objects and asyncio queues, events and futures are not thread safe. Code in another thread must not call loop.call_soon or set a future's result directly. Use loop.call_soon_threadsafe to schedule a callback, or asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe to submit a coroutine and get a concurrent.futures.Future back.

D3. Closing Asynchronous Generators: An async generator that holds a resource needs to be closed. Leaving an async for loop early with break does not by itself run the generator's finally block at that moment; finalisation is scheduled by the loop later. Use contextlib.aclosing or call await agen.aclose() explicitly to release connections deterministically.

D4. Entering the Loop from Synchronous Code: asyncio.run(main()) creates a new event loop, runs the coroutine to completion and closes the loop. It raises RuntimeError if called while a loop is already running in the same thread, which is the normal situation inside an IPython kernel or a web framework handler. In such environments await the coroutine directly or schedule it on the existing loop.

D5. Task References and Collection: The event loop keeps only a weak reference to tasks created with create_task. A task whose result is never stored may be collected while suspended, and it then disappears without an exception. Keep strong references, for example in a set, and remove each task with a done callback. Awaiting the task or using a TaskGroup also keeps it alive.

D6. Liveness and Readiness Probes: A failing readiness probe removes the pod from Service endpoints but keeps it running. A failing liveness probe makes the kubelet restart the container. Slow starting applications should use a startupProbe so that liveness checks do not kill them before they are initialised.

D7. Per-Task Context Variables: contextvars.ContextVar values are copied into a task when it is created. Changes made inside the task stay local to it and are not visible to the parent, which is why frameworks use them for request identifiers or tracing spans. A value set after create_task is called is not seen by that task.

D8. Error Propagation in gather and TaskGroup: asyncio.gather with the default settings raises the first exception to the caller, but the other awaitables keep running in the background. With return_exceptions=True exceptions are returned as results instead. A TaskGroup behaves differently: when one child fails, the remaining children are cancelled and the failures are raised together as an ExceptionGroup, which is caught with except*.

D9. no-cache Versus no-store: Cache-Control: no-cache does not forbid storing: it requires the cache to revalidate with the origin before every reuse. no-store forbids storing the response at all, which is appropriate for sensitive data. Confusing the two is a common cause of either stale or needlessly uncached pages.

D10. How Cancellation Is Delivered: Calling task.cancel() does not stop the coroutine immediately: it schedules a CancelledError to be raised at the next await point. Since Python 3.8 CancelledError derives from BaseException, so a bare except Exception no longer swallows it, but a bare except or except BaseException will. Cleanup code should use try/finally, and if the error is caught it must normally be re-raised so the task really ends as cancelled.

D11. Bounded Queues as Backpressure: An asyncio.Queue created without maxsize accepts unlimited items, so a fast producer can fill memory while a slow consumer lags. With maxsize=N, put() waits when the queue is full, which slows the producer to the consumer's pace. Consumers call task_done() after each item so that join() can tell when everything has been processed.

D12. Coroutine Objects That Never Run: Calling an async function returns a coroutine object; the body does not run until the coroutine is awaited or wrapped in a task. Forgetting the await leaves the work undone and produces a 'coroutine was never awaited' RuntimeWarning when the object is garbage collected. Static checkers and the -X dev mode help catch it. The returned object is truthy, so conditions on it silently pass.

D13. Denormal Numbers and Underflow: Values closer to zero than the smallest normal double are stored as denormal numbers with reduced precision, and operations on them can be dramatically slower on some processors. Results smaller still flush to zero. Scaling data or enabling flush-to-zero modes avoids the slowdown.

D14. Synchronous Calls Inside Coroutines: The event loop runs all tasks on one thread, so a coroutine that makes a blocking call (time.sleep, requests.get, a CPU-heavy parse) stops every other task until it returns. Await-based equivalents such as asyncio.sleep or an async HTTP client let the loop switch tasks. For code that cannot be made async, hand it to a worker with asyncio.to_thread or loop.run_in_executor. Profiling with the loop's debug mode reports callbacks that take longer than 100 ms.

D15. Node Affinity and Selectors: A nodeSelector or requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution node affinity restricts a pod to nodes whose labels match. If no node has the required labels, the pod stays Pending with an event stating that no nodes matched the node affinity or selector. Preferred affinities only influence scoring.

D16. Bounding Concurrent Work: Starting ten thousand requests at once can exhaust sockets or overwhelm a server. An asyncio.Semaphore initialised to N lets at most N coroutines pass through an async with block at the same time; others wait their turn. Create the semaphore inside the running loop's context and share it between the tasks that must be limited together.

  1.3 If any provision of this scheme is found to be invalid or unenforceable by a court of competent jurisdiction, the remaining provisions shall remain in full force and effect. This scheme represents the entire agreement regarding the reimbursement of medical costs and supersedes any prior verbal or written agreements.

2. COVERAGE AND LIMITS
  2.1 The scheme covers the following categories:
  - Primary Care Visits: Covers consultations with general practitioners, pediatricians, and other primary care physicians for diagnosis and treatment of acute conditions. Per-event limit: €2,500.
  - Prescription Medications: Covers the cost of medications prescribed by a licensed healthcare provider for the treatment of a covered condition. Per-event limit: €750.
  - Diagnostic Laboratory Tests: Covers blood tests, urine tests, and other laboratory analyses ordered by a physician to diagnose or monitor a medical condition. Per-event limit: €250.
  - Emergency Room Treatment: Covers treatment received at a hospital emergency department for a sudden, severe, or life-threatening condition, including stabilization and initial care. Per-event limit: €250.
  2.2 The deductible of €300 is subtracted from the loss before the per-event limit is applied.
  2.3 The employee bears 20% of the amount remaining after the deductible and limit; the provider pays the rest.
  2.4 Total payments in one policy year may not exceed €20,000; amounts already paid in the year reduce what remains.

3. EXCLUSIONS
  3.1 Any procedure performed primarily for aesthetic purposes, including but not limited to cosmetic surgery, laser resurfacing, or liposuction, is excluded unless medically necessary to restore function or treat an injury.
  3.2 Medications that are available without a prescription, such as pain relievers, antihistamines, or vitamins, are excluded from reimbursement even if recommended by a physician.
  3.3 Routine dental check-ups, cleanings, fillings, extractions, and routine eye exams or corrective lenses are excluded, unless required due to an accidental injury or a covered illness.
  3.4 Medical services received outside the European Economic Area (EEA) are excluded, except in cases of emergency care required during business travel.

4. CONDITIONS
  4.1 Nothing is payable for a loss occurring fewer than 14 days after the inception date.
  4.2 A reimbursement request must be notified within 14 days after the loss date; later notification is not accepted.
  4.3 Every reimbursement request must be accompanied by the itemized invoice from the healthcare provider.

5. ASSESSMENT PROCEDURE
  Each reimbursement request is assessed in this order and the first applicable step decides it: (a) waiting period (4.1), (b) notification deadline (4.2), (c) exclusions (Section 3; the lowest-numbered applicable exclusion is named), (d) documentation (4.3: the reimbursement request is held, not denied), (e) amount (Section 2), (f) any amount above €800 requires senior-adjuster sign-off before payment.

6. PRECEDENCE
  If any other part of these terms conflicts with Section 3 or Section 5, Sections 3 and 5 prevail.
  If you have questions about this scheme, you may contact our support team by email at support@medireturn.example or by telephone at the number printed on your employee benefits card. Our operating hours are from nine in the morning to five in the afternoon, Monday through Friday.

7. ADMINISTRATION
  7.1 We process personal data in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation. Your medical and financial information is used solely for assessing and paying your reimbursement request and is shared only with the employer and relevant service providers as necessary. We retain records for the duration required by law.
  7.2 In this scheme, 'you' refers to the employee who is eligible under the terms of your employment contract. 1. DEFINITIONS AND GENERAL TERMS
  1.1 If you are unhappy with our service, contact our Customer Relations team in writing and explain what happened. We will review your concerns and tell you how to refer the matter to the appropriate independent complaints body.

2. COVERAGE AND LIMITS
  2.1 The scheme covers the following categories:
  - Business premises: Covers insured physical damage to the building used for the policyholder’s business. Per-event limit: £500.
  - Business contents: Covers insured physical damage to furniture, furnishings, and other business contents at the premises. Per-event limit: £250.
  - Stock: Covers insured physical damage to goods held for sale or used in the policyholder’s trade. Per-event limit: £500.
  - Business equipment: Covers insured physical damage to tools, machinery, and office equipment used in the business. Per-event limit: £400.
  2.2 The per-event limit is applied to the loss first; the deductible of £50 is then subtracted from the capped amount.
  2.3 The policyholder bears 25% of the amount remaining after the deductible and limit; the provider pays the rest.
  2.4 Total payments in one policy year may not exceed £3,000; amounts already paid in the year reduce what remains.

3. EXCLUSIONS
  3.1 We do not cover damage caused by gradual deterioration, corrosion, or an ongoing leak.
  3.2 We do not cover damage to property directly caused by faulty design, materials, or workmanship.
  3.3 We do not cover damage deliberately caused by the policyholder or someone acting with the policyholder’s consent.
  3.4 We do not cover damage occurring while the premises are left unoccupied for an extended period without our written agreement.

4. CONDITIONS
  4.1 Nothing is payable for a loss occurring fewer than 30 days after the inception date.
  4.2 A claim must be notified within 30 days after the loss date; later notification is not accepted.
  4.3 Every claim must be accompanied by the Itemised repair invoice.

5. ASSESSMENT PROCEDURE

6. PRECEDENCE
  If any other part of these terms conflicts with Section 3 or Section 5, Sections 3 and 5 prevail.
  We use the information you provide to administer your cover, handle claims, and meet our legal responsibilities. We may share relevant information with professional advisers and service providers who support those activities.

7. ADMINISTRATION
  7.1 A policyholder may make a claim, or may authorise a representative to communicate with us about it. Please tell us if your representative’s authority changes.
  7.2 If any part of this document is found to be unenforceable, the remaining provisions will continue to apply. This document should be read together with your schedule and any endorsements.

On May 14, inspector Lena Voss visited the Cedar Spoon Café at 18 Alder Street for a routine food-safety inspection. The café received a score of 86 out of 100. In the prep area, the inspector measured the reach-in refrigerator at 46°F; the required maximum was 41°F. The manager moved the stored chicken to a working refrigerator, and a follow-up temperature reading there was 38°F. The inspector also observed that a container of sliced tomatoes had no date label. Staff labeled it during the visit, and the manager said the tomatoes had been prepared that morning.

The handwashing sink beside the dishwashing area was blocked by two boxes of paper cups. An employee moved the boxes after the inspector pointed out the obstruction. Voss noted that the sink was accessible before she left. No pest activity was observed in the kitchen or storage room, and the café’s sanitizer test strips were available and in date.

The inspection report classified the refrigerator temperature and blocked sink as priority violations. The missing date label was recorded as a minor violation. The manager was given until May 21 to submit documentation that the refrigerator had been repaired or replaced. A reinspection was scheduled for May 28. The report did not require a closure, and the café remained open after the visit. Voss advised the manager to check and record refrigerator temperatures at the beginning and end of each workday until the follow-up inspection.

A volunteer group had three jobs to fill, and three helpers, Greta, Viktor and Hana, each of whom would take exactly one. The jobs were running the field survey in the mountains (done in the big tent); painting and building the set (done in the big tent); preparing and giving the final presentation (done in the lobby). The organiser wanted the allocation that used everyone's strengths and avoided friction.

Greta lived alone, kept long hours and was known for bringing home-baked biscuits to meetings. Greta had spent two summers painting scenery for an opera company and knew every trick for covering a large surface quickly. Greta had taught evening classes for years and was comfortable in front of an audience. Greta disliked camping and had cut the last expedition short. A colleague who was not involved passed through twice, whistling.

Viktor had been with the organisation for 12 years and was generally regarded as reliable, if a little reserved. Viktor read slides word for word in a monotone that put people to sleep. Viktor had spent two summers painting scenery for an opera company and knew every trick for covering a large surface quickly. Viktor had done fieldwork in remote areas and enjoyed long days outdoors. Someone had left a half-finished cup of coffee on the nearest surface.

Hana was an early riser and often the first to arrive, which had caused a few friendly jokes. Hana could manage an easy hike but not a multi-day trek. Hana feared speaking to professors and would panic in a large hall. Hana was colour-blind and had once painted a tree trunk bright green. The radio was playing an old song nobody could name.

Greta and Viktor had fallen out badly some months earlier, and neither would agree to work in the same room as the other for any length of time. Nobody else had any difficulty with anybody.

state.story:
• Interner Vorfall im Abrechnungsteam
• Ermittlungsnotiz der Helpdesk-Leitung

Als die Frühschicht im Telekommunikations-Helpdesk eintraf, lag die zuständige Abrechnungsfachkraft verletzt im schmalen Verbindungsgang hinter dem Büroraum. Sie war bei Bewusstsein, konnte jedoch zunächst nur stockend sprechen. Der Rettungsdienst brachte sie zur Untersuchung fort. Der Gang führte auch zum verschlossenen Lagerraum, in dem ein Spezialwerkzeug aufbewahrt wurde. Die Polizei bat die interne Ermittlerin, Zugangsprotokolle und Aussagen zu sichern, bevor der Betrieb den Bereich wieder freigab.

Der Vorfall hatte sich während einer kritischen halben Stunde ereignet. Die Ermittlerin ließ deshalb für diesen Zeitraum die Gebäudezugänge, die Überwachung und die Arbeitsabläufe prüfen. Ein beschädigtes Gehäuse lag neben der verletzten Fachkraft; die Spuren deuteten darauf hin, dass das Werkzeug aus dem Lagerraum benutzt worden war. Ob der Angriff geplant gewesen war oder aus einer Auseinandersetzung heraus geschah, ließ sich am Fundort nicht erkennen. Auch ein offener Abrechnungsfall, über den im Team gestritten worden war, erwies sich zunächst als wenig aussagekräftig: Mehrere Personen hatten daran gearbeitet.

Tomás Navarro wurde befragt, weil er am Vortag den einzigen Generalschlüsselcode ausgeliehen hatte. Die Ausgabe war im internen Register vermerkt, und Tomás bestätigte die Entleihung. Auf die Frage nach seinem Verhältnis zur verletzten Fachkraft erklärte er, zwischen ihnen habe es keinen Streit gegeben. Die Prüfung der Kamerabilder ergab zudem, dass Tomás während der gesamten kritischen halben Stunde an einem anderen Standort zu sehen war. Die Aufnahmen ließen keine Unterbrechung erkennen, in der er hätte zum Helpdesk gelangen können.

Owen Pritchard kannte sich mit dem Spezialwerkzeug aus. In seiner Aussage erklärte er, im Umgang damit geschult worden zu sein; eine Kollegin bestätigte, dass er regelmäßig bei technischen Arbeiten half. Zugleich schilderten mehrere Beschäftigte sein Verhältnis zur verletzten Fachkraft als ausgesprochen gut. Owen hatte ihr Geld geliehen, als sie vor kurzem Schwierigkeiten gehabt hatte. Für den fraglichen Zeitraum fand die Ermittlerin jedoch niemanden, der bestätigen konnte, wo Owen gewesen war. Er sagte, er habe sich im Gebäude bewegt und niemandem Rechenschaft über jeden seiner Schritte abgelegt. Eine Kamera erfasste ihn dort nicht eindeutig.

Aiko Tanaka hatte Zugang zum Lagerraum, denn sie besaß einen Schlüssel zu dessen Tür. Die Ermittlerin stellte fest, dass der Schlüssel zu den ausgegebenen Berechtigungen gehörte; ein gewaltsames Öffnen der Tür war nicht erforderlich gewesen. Im Gespräch erinnerte Aiko daran, dass die verletzte Fachkraft sie im vergangenen Monat vor anderen Beschäftigten bloßgestellt hatte. Sie beschrieb den Vorfall als demütigend und sagte, sie habe sich danach aus den Gesprächen im Team zurückgezogen. Das Zugangsprotokoll zeigte, dass Aiko wenige Minuten vor dem Vorfall im Gebäude ein- und erst nach dem Vorfall wieder ausgetragen worden war.

Auch Lucía Ferreira hatte am Vortag den einzigen Generalschlüsselcode ausgeliehen. Das Register führte ihre Entleihung ebenso auf wie die von Tomás. Lucía bestritt, mit der verletzten Fachkraft zerstritten zu sein. Nach den Aussagen der Teammitglieder waren beide vielmehr gut miteinander ausgekommen; Lucía hatte der Fachkraft Geld geliehen. Ihr Zugangsausweis wurde wenige Minuten vor dem Vorfall am Gebäude registriert, und der Ausgangseintrag erfolgte erst danach. Lucía sagte, sie habe sich währenddessen im Arbeitsbereich aufgehalten, konnte aber keine Person nennen, die ihren Weg durch das Gebäude beobachtet hatte.

Die Ermittlerin prüfte außerdem zwei Ablenkungen. Ein fehlendes Ladegerät tauchte noch während der Befragungen in einer Schublade auf; es hatte keinen Bezug zum Angriff. Ebenso meldete ein Beschäftigter einen verdächtigen Anruf, doch die Verbindung stammte aus einer automatischen Kundenabfrage und führte zu keinem der Befragten. Die Polizei sicherte das Werkzeug und nahm die Aussagen auf. Für die interne Entscheidung blieben damit die persönlichen Beziehungen, die verfügbaren Zugänge und die belegbaren Aufenthaltsorte im fraglichen Zeitraum maßgeblich. Die Ermittlerin legte ihre Unterlagen der Helpdesk-Leitung vor, ohne die Schlussfolgerung in den Vermerk aufzunehmen.

Ravi Navarro, the senior chemist at the Skarsgaard research station, was found collapsed in the stockroom shortly before five on Saturday afternoon. A toxicologist later found that a cup of tea at Ravi Navarro's elbow had been laced with a fast-acting sedative, and that the quantity taken was enough to have caused respiratory failure. Detective Sergeant Ibarra spent two days taking statements from the staff who had been on site that weekend.

The people of interest were Maya, the station manager, Selin, the cook, and Yara, the lab technician.

The weekly delivery of fresh vegetables had arrived two days late. The station's generator had cut out twice that month, and staff blamed the new freezer. A seal had been spotted on the rocks, which drew half the staff to the windows for most of the morning.

Selin had been secretly reporting Ravi's mistakes to the funder and feared that Ravi had found out. Selin was trained in handling controlled substances and had signed one out two weeks earlier. Yara was due to take a holiday the following week and had spent days handing work over. Yara had once been mentioned in a complaint, but it had been withdrawn two years earlier and had nothing to do with Ravi. Yara had just received a glowing reference from Ravi and was due to move on to a better job. The weekly delivery of fresh vegetables had arrived two days late.

Yara kept the station's medicine cabinet, which held the sedative, and was the only one with a key. Maya had been passed over for the project lead in favour of Ravi, and had said so loudly at the last staff meeting. Yara was seen leaving the stockroom area around ten past four, hurrying and not answering when greeted. Selin had left the island on the 3:30 boat and was filmed by the ferry's camera. The station's generator had cut out twice that month, and staff blamed the new freezer.

Selin had a reputation for meticulous note-taking and for never raising a voice in an argument. Several colleagues thought Selin had behaved oddly afterwards, but it emerged that Selin had simply been shaken by the news. Maya was an early riser and often the first to arrive, which had caused a few friendly jokes. Maya had made Ravi's tea that day, as Maya did every afternoon, and carried it to the stockroom. Maya had no one to vouch for the afternoon; the station's door log showed nothing between 3:50 and 4:50. Someone had left an old anorak in the stockroom, and it had been the subject of a joke for a week.

Detective Sergeant Ibarra put the notes in order and began to draft a report.

state.story:
Reference K-17. The kitchen had been stripped to bare boards, with cabinet doors stacked against the dining-room wall and a temporary worktop balanced over trestles. The household had kept the old pantry storeroom locked while the renovation was underway. A powered cutting tool and several fittings were kept inside. The victim, who was supervising the work, was found injured beside the temporary worktop after the tool had been used. The injury was serious enough to require medical attention, but the victim survived. No one in the household had seen the blow land.

Inspector Vale arrived while dust still coated the hall. The tool lay on its side near the pantry entrance. The storeroom door was shut again, its lock intact. The inspector kept the household away from the work area and asked the building manager to preserve the sign-in book. The victim could not give a reliable account of the incident. The inspector therefore began with people who had been in or near the building and with the records that could establish what they knew and where they had been.

Aiko Tanaka had been helping with the renovation’s household arrangements. The victim’s absence would not have improved Aiko’s position or brought Aiko any benefit; Aiko said they had been trying to keep the work on schedule. The building manager confirmed that Aiko had never been given access to the locked storeroom and had no key. Aiko described spending the relevant period moving between the kitchen and the front hall. Nobody could confirm Aiko’s whereabouts during the critical half hour. Aiko’s account did not establish where they had been throughout it.

Ingrid Solberg had argued with the victim in front of workers last month. Two people who heard the exchange said the victim had embarrassed Ingrid openly, and Ingrid had left without answering. Ingrid told the inspector she had been angry, but said she had come back to discuss the kitchen work. The sign-in book showed Ingrid entering the building a few minutes before the incident; the building manager saw her leave after it. The tool was a powered model with controls requiring trained handling. The contractor responsible for it said Ingrid had never been taught to operate it and was not trained for that task.

Greta Vogel had a separate dispute with the victim. Her messages and the victim’s ledger both showed that the victim owed her a large sum. Greta did not deny the debt. The building manager also confirmed that Greta possessed a key to the locked storeroom, where the powered tool had been kept. Greta’s name appeared in the sign-in book a few minutes before the incident, and the manager recalled her leaving after it. She said she had come to settle the account and had not entered the kitchen. The inspector noted the statement without treating it as proof of where Greta had been.

Tomás Navarro had been trusted with private information by the victim. A message recovered from the victim’s phone showed that Tomás had recently learned the victim was leaking their secrets. Tomás was plainly unsettled when asked about it and said the disclosure had damaged the trust between them. The contractor’s access record showed that Tomás had handed back their code a week earlier. The code no longer opened the storeroom. Like Aiko, Tomás had no one who could account for their movements during the critical half hour.

The inspector also checked two details that seemed dramatic but led nowhere. A cracked ceramic tile had been found beside the work area, but the installer said it had cracked during removal and had no connection to the injury. A delivery driver had left a box of brass handles in the hall; the receipt and the driver’s route confirmed the delivery, and nothing was missing. Neither detail altered the accounts, the lock, or the sign-in record.

Vale returned to the pantry door and examined the tool’s storage place. The lock had not been forced. The sign-in book established arrivals and departures, not what anyone had done between them. The inspector laid out the interviews, the access information, and the contractor’s account of who could use the tool. In the kitchen, the victim’s unfinished cabinets waited beneath a strip of masking tape. Vale closed the notebook and asked for the case file to be kept open.

马罗角帆船俱乐部会长罗莎·博伊德于星期六傍晚被发现倒在俱乐部浮桥尽头，头部受伤；附近的木板上放着一支船钩。俱乐部当天举办了夏季帆船赛，许多人都在俱乐部场地内。警督科尔尼着手查明谁可能曾与罗莎·博伊德单独待在浮桥上。

竞争对手、船长菲利克斯也在接受询问的人之列。菲利克斯以做笔记一丝不苟、争论时从不提高嗓门而闻名。菲利克斯发现罗莎挪用了俱乐部资金，并被告知要保持沉默。菲利克斯熟悉浮桥的布局，也知道摄像头的盲区在哪里。有人看到菲利克斯在差二十分六点时朝浮桥走去，直到警报响起才再次有人看到他。傍晚的风停了，这让参赛者们很失望。

烧烤摊在六点前就把香肠卖完了。一阵短暂的毛毛雨让野餐的人们在五点左右进了俱乐部会所。抽奖因失误进行了两次，中奖者也让人搞不清楚。

酒吧经理魏也在接受询问的人之列。魏以做笔记一丝不苟、争论时从不提高嗓门而闻名。魏说自己当时在酒吧，但酒保说魏在五点半左右就离开了。当天早上，罗莎因魏违反安全规定而禁止魏参加帆船赛，魏对此愤怒不已。魏双臂做过手术后，力气不足以抬起船钩。抽奖因失误进行了两次，中奖者也让人搞不清楚。

Zainab Lindholm, owner of Mill Lane Bakery, was found at ten to five on Monday morning in the flour store behind the shop, having been struck by a heavy rolling pin. The bakery's night shift had been at work, and the back door had been unlocked. Detective Constable Singh questioned everyone with a link to the bakery.

The people of interest were Greta, the apprentice, Viktor, a rival baker, Noah, the owner's business partner, and Marcus, the landlord.

The oven timer had been broken for a week, which made the head baker grumpy. The shop's chalkboard had listed a pastry that no longer existed. A flour delivery had arrived with the wrong grade and been sent back.

Greta had a reputation for meticulous note-taking and for never raising a voice in an argument. Several colleagues thought Greta had behaved oddly afterwards, but it emerged that Greta had simply been shaken by the news. Viktor was due to take a holiday the following week and had spent days handing work over. Noah had moved to the area 11 years earlier and was still considered a newcomer by some. Marcus had recently taken up long-distance running and talked about little else at lunch. A rumour that Marcus had been arguing loudly in the car park the day before turned out to be about a disputed parking space and nothing more.

On the question of access and means, the inspector heard the following. Greta had keys to the back door and the flour store, and handled the rolling pins every day. Viktor had never been to the back of the bakery and did not know the layout. Marcus knew where the CCTV was switched off in the back yard. Noah was seen sharpening and adjusting the heavy rolling pins the afternoon before.

A flour delivery had arrived with the wrong grade and been sent back.

On the question of motives, the inspector heard the following. Marcus had joined the week before and had no complaint. Greta had a good relationship with Zainab and had signed a long, comfortable new contract. Noah was owed three months of wages and had been fobbed off by Zainab. Viktor had been told by Zainab that the lease would not be renewed, which would end Viktor's trade on the street.

The shop's chalkboard had listed a pastry that no longer existed.

On the question of who could have been present, the inspector heard the following. Viktor was seen letting themselves in by the back door around 4:20. Noah could not say where they were between four and five, and the phone records showed the phone switched off. Greta was on the night shift at the hospital with a time clock for each break. Marcus's van was parked in the back lane at twenty past four, according to a neighbour.

A pigeon had been nesting above the back door and nobody had the heart to move it.

Detective Constable Singh put the notes in order and began to draft a report.

Rule 2: when door_nursery becomes closed and the current mode is night: set lock_hall=locked
Rule 3: when lock_hall becomes unlocked: set office_heat=17
Rule 4: when motion is detected in attic: set nursery_plug=on, attic_plug=off
Rule 5: when the mode becomes movie: set nursery_heat=15, lock_nursery=locked
Rule 6 (once): when the mode becomes guest: set kitchen_blind=open, nursery_blind=closed, kitchen_light=on@100
