RESIDENTIAL TENANCY DEPOSIT RETURN POLICY
Issued by Willow Quay Lettings Trust


1. DEFINITIONS AND GENERAL TERMS
  1.1 Applications and supporting records may be sent through the tenant portal or delivered to the Trust's correspondence address shown on the tenancy agreement. The Trust can also be contacted through the deposit team using the contact details provided with the account information.
  1.2 For this policy, the deposit is the tenancy security sum held by Willow Quay Lettings Trust in connection with a residential tenancy. The tenancy checkout report records the property's condition and the return of its fixtures and keys.
  1.3 The Trust uses personal information and tenancy records to administer deposit returns, communicate with tenants, and maintain its property accounts. Information is handled by staff and service providers who need it for those purposes, in accordance with the Trust's privacy notice.

2. COVERAGE AND LIMITS
  2.1 The scheme covers the following categories:
  - Remaining deposit balance: This covers the return of the deposit balance after agreed tenancy charges have been accounted for. Per-event limit: £400.
  - Rent reconciliation: This covers deposit adjustments relating to rent recorded as unpaid at the end of the tenancy. Per-event limit: £250.
  - Property condition: This covers deposit adjustments for tenant-caused damage beyond ordinary wear and tear. Per-event limit: £500.
  - Cleaning and keys: This covers deposit adjustments for required cleaning or unreturned property keys. Per-event limit: £1,000.
  2.2 The deductible of £150 is subtracted from the loss before the per-event limit is applied.
  2.3 The tenant bears 25% of the amount remaining after the deductible and limit; the provider pays the rest.
  2.4 Total payments in one policy year may not exceed £12,000; amounts already paid in the year reduce what remains.

3. EXCLUSIONS
  3.1 A tenant cannot be charged for deterioration caused by ordinary use when the tenancy ended.
  3.2 Damage documented before the tenant took possession cannot be charged to that tenant.
  3.3 A proposed deduction cannot be made where the landlord has not provided evidence of the cost incurred.
  3.4 A repair or service cost cannot be charged to the tenant when it arose from the landlord's legal responsibility to maintain the property.

4. CONDITIONS
  4.1 Nothing is payable for a loss occurring fewer than 30 days after the inception date.
  4.2 A application must be notified within 7 days after the loss date; later notification is not accepted.
  4.3 Every application must be accompanied by the Signed tenancy checkout report.

5. ASSESSMENT PROCEDURE
  Each application is assessed in this order and the first applicable step decides it: (a) waiting period (4.1), (b) notification deadline (4.2), (c) exclusions (Section 3; the lowest-numbered applicable exclusion is named), (d) documentation (4.3: the application is held, not denied), (e) amount (Section 2), (f) any amount above £1,500 requires senior-adjuster sign-off before payment.

6. PRECEDENCE
  If any other part of these terms conflicts with Section 3 or Section 5, Sections 3 and 5 prevail.
  A tenant named on the tenancy agreement may make an application for the return of the deposit. Where several tenants are named, they may identify one tenant to communicate with the Trust on their behalf.

7. ADMINISTRATION
  7.1 A tenant who is dissatisfied with the handling of an application may write to the Trust's complaints team and describe the concern and the outcome sought. The team will record the complaint and provide a written response through the tenant's chosen contact channel.
  7.2 If any part of this policy is found to be unenforceable, the remaining provisions continue to apply. The affected provision will be read as closely as possible to its original purpose while respecting applicable tenancy law.

A rule with a condition fires only if the condition holds at that moment; a rule marked "once" fires only the first time its trigger and condition match.

A direct user command sets the device and puts it on manual hold. Automation actions on a held device are skipped until the next "mode" event, which releases all holds before its rules fire. Commands do not trigger rules by themselves.
A lock cannot be set to locked while its door sensor reads open: the action is ignored (the lock keeps its value, and no change happens). Unlocking is always possible.
Thermostat setpoints (heat devices) are limited to the range 18-24: a larger or smaller value is stored as the nearest limit.

When a device actually changes value (caused by a user command or by a rule; no change if it already had that value), rules with trigger "device becomes value" are queued and fire after the current event's own rules, in the order the changes happened.
Value codes: on@N = light on at N % brightness, off, on/off for plugs, locked/unlocked, open/closed for blinds, a number = thermostat setpoint in °C.

state.story:
Registro della bottega — sera dell’incidente

Quando arrivò la chiamata, il laboratorio di ceramica era già stato svuotato dai corsi serali. Il commissario Serra trovò la porta dell’area di lavorazione aperta e una striscia di argilla schiacciata sul pavimento. Marta Valli, responsabile del laboratorio, era stata colpita alla testa accanto alla pressa per lastre. Respirava, ma non riusciva a parlare; i soccorritori la portarono via e l’investigatore cominciò a ricostruire ciò che era successo durante la mezz’ora decisiva.

La pressa era un macchinario pesante, usato per assottigliare l’argilla prima della cottura. Secondo la scheda di manutenzione, non presentava guasti. Il tecnico spiegò che qualcuno aveva spostato la leva di sicurezza e che per manovrare correttamente quel macchinario serviva addestramento. Serra controllò i registri del laboratorio e i colloqui con il personale: non cercava una lite generica, ma una persona che avesse avuto una ragione per affrontare Marta, sapesse usare la pressa e potesse essere stata lì quando lei era rimasta sola.

Owen Pritchard lavorava da anni nella bottega. Disse di aver avuto una discussione con Marta sulla gestione dei turni, ma non aggiunse altro. Una collega, sentita separatamente, riferì che Owen si aspettava una promozione e che Marta era stata scelta al suo posto. Nei registri di formazione figurava anche il suo addestramento all’uso della pressa; Owen aveva imparato a regolarla e a intervenire sulla leva senza rischiare di bloccarla. Per la mezz’ora in cui Marta era stata ferita, però, nessuno seppe dire di aver visto Owen altrove o di essere rimasto con lui. Serra annotò la mancanza di una conferma, senza trasformarla in una prova.

Ingrid Solberg era stata interrogata nel cortile, mentre aspettava un passaggio. Aveva lasciato il laboratorio prima che cominciasse la mezz’ora critica: il registro della porta e la testimonianza del custode concordavano. Ingrid aveva anche restituito il proprio codice d’accesso una settimana prima. Non risultò che la scomparsa di Marta le avrebbe portato vantaggi; anzi, le sue commesse dipendevano dall’apertura regolare della bottega. Il suo nome comparve comunque nel taccuino di Serra, perché aveva avuto contrasti con la responsabile sulle consegne, ma quel dissenso non cambiava i dati verificati.

Dana Whitlock, come Owen, aveva sperato di ottenere la promozione assegnata a Marta. Anche lei aveva seguito la formazione necessaria per usare la pressa. In questo caso, tuttavia, le registrazioni di sorveglianza erano nette: per tutta la mezz’ora dell’incidente Dana si trovava in un altro sito, ripresa dalle telecamere all’ingresso e nell’area di lavoro. Serra fece controllare gli orari e parlò con chi custodiva le immagini. Non c’erano interruzioni nel filmato né spostamenti che potessero riportarla alla bottega.

Aiko Tanaka arrivò con un avvocato e una cartella di fatture. Disse che Marta le doveva una somma considerevole per una fornitura di argille speciali. Un registro della bottega confermava inoltre che Aiko aveva preso in prestito il codice principale il giorno prima dell’incidente. Il responsabile dei corsi, però, raccontò che durante la mezz’ora in questione Aiko stava tenendo una presentazione davanti a una sala piena di colleghi. I presenti confermarono il racconto; anche una ripresa della sala mostrava Aiko mentre parlava. La cartella conteneva ricevute contestate, un dettaglio che Serra giudicò utile per capire il rapporto tra i due, non per alterare ciò che era accaduto quella sera.

Priya Raman fu l’ultima a essere ascoltata. Aveva scoperto che Marta stava rivelando ad altri alcune informazioni riservate che le aveva confidato. Priya ne era rimasta ferita e aveva affrontato la responsabile, come dimostrava un messaggio letto da Serra. Ma Priya non aveva mai ricevuto istruzioni per usare la pressa e non era stata formata a manovrarla. Quanto alla mezz’ora dell’incidente, nessuno seppe indicare dove fosse: non c’era una persona che potesse confermare la sua presenza in un altro luogo.

Serra chiuse il taccuino. Le testimonianze, i registri e le immagini non avevano lo stesso peso, e alcuni dissapori erano soltanto rumore. La pressa restava immobile sotto i neon, mentre dalla sala dei torni arrivava il ticchettio dell’acqua nel lavandino. Prima di lasciare la bottega, l’investigatore chiese che il macchinario e i registri d’accesso fossero conservati intatti.

A rule with a condition fires only if the condition holds at that moment; a rule marked "once" fires only the first time its trigger and condition match.

A direct user command sets the device and puts it on manual hold. Automation actions on a held device are skipped until the next "mode" event, which releases all holds before its rules fire. Commands do not trigger rules by themselves.
A lock cannot be set to locked while its door sensor reads open: the action is ignored (the lock keeps its value, and no change happens). Unlocking is always possible.
Thermostat setpoints (heat devices) are limited to the range 17-25: a larger or smaller value is stored as the nearest limit.

When a device actually changes value (caused by a user command or by a rule; no change if it already had that value), rules with trigger "device becomes value" are queued and fire after the current event's own rules, in the order the changes happened.
Value codes: on@N = light on at N % brightness, off, on/off for plugs, locked/unlocked, open/closed for blinds, a number = thermostat setpoint in °C.

EMPLOYEE RELOCATION ASSISTANCE POLICY
Issued by Northstar People Services


1. DEFINITIONS AND GENERAL TERMS
  1.1 Employees can contact the People Services Relocation Desk through the staff portal or by writing to relocation@northstar.example. The desk can explain the submission process and help identify the information needed for a request.
  1.2 An employee assigned by Northstar People Services to a new work location may make a reimbursement request under this policy. The request should identify the relocation and describe the expense being submitted.
  1.3 Northstar People Services uses information in a request to administer relocation assistance, verify expenses, and maintain its records. Access is restricted to staff who need the information for those tasks, and personal information is handled under the organisation’s privacy practices.

2. COVERAGE AND LIMITS
  2.1 The scheme covers the following categories:
  - Household move: Covers professional packing, transport, and delivery of the employee’s household belongings to the new residence. Per-event limit: €5,000.
  - Relocation travel: Covers reasonable transport costs for the employee and eligible accompanying family members traveling to the new work location. Per-event limit: €250.
  - Temporary accommodation: Covers short-term lodging while the employee arranges permanent housing near the new work location. Per-event limit: €5,000.
  - Household storage: Covers storage of household belongings when the new residence is not ready to receive them. Per-event limit: €1,000.
  2.2 The per-event limit is applied to the loss first; the deductible of €200 is then subtracted from the capped amount.
  2.3 The employee bears 20% of the amount remaining after the deductible and limit; the provider pays the rest.
  2.4 Total payments in one policy year may not exceed €10,000; amounts already paid in the year reduce what remains.

3. EXCLUSIONS
  3.1 Personal purchases are excluded when they are not necessary to move or settle the employee’s household at the new work location.
  3.2 Ordinary commuting costs are excluded when they relate to regular travel between the employee’s residence and workplace after the relocation.
  3.3 Travel costs for guests are excluded when the travelers are not the employee or eligible accompanying family members.
  3.4 Storage costs are excluded when the employee chose storage despite the new residence being ready to receive the household belongings.

4. CONDITIONS
  4.1 Nothing is payable for a loss occurring fewer than 14 days after the inception date.
  4.2 A reimbursement request must be notified within 21 days after the loss date; later notification is not accepted.
  4.3 Every reimbursement request must be accompanied by the Itemized supplier invoice.

5. ASSESSMENT PROCEDURE
  Each reimbursement request is assessed in this order and the first applicable step decides it: (a) waiting period (4.1), (b) notification deadline (4.2), (c) exclusions (Section 3; the lowest-numbered applicable exclusion is named), (d) documentation (4.3: the reimbursement request is held, not denied), (e) amount (Section 2), (f) any amount above €1,200 requires senior-adjuster sign-off before payment.

6. PRECEDENCE
  If any other part of these terms conflicts with Section 3 or Section 5, Sections 3 and 5 prevail.
  If a provision of this policy is found unenforceable, the remaining provisions continue to apply. The affected provision will be interpreted as closely as possible to its original purpose where permitted by law.

7. ADMINISTRATION
  7.1 An employee who is dissatisfied with the way a request was handled may send a written complaint to the People Services Review Team through the staff portal. The team will consider the concerns and provide a written response.
  7.2 For this policy, relocation means a move required by a change in the employee’s assigned work location. Household belongings means personal property ordinarily kept in the employee’s home.

1. Definitions. “Confidential Information” means all information, in any form (written, oral, electronic or visual), that the Disclosing Party discloses to the Receiving Party in connection with the Purpose, whether or not it is marked as confidential.

2. Scope of disclosure. Each party may disclose Confidential Information to the other party, and each party is a Receiving Party in respect of the Confidential Information it receives.

3. Export control. Each party shall comply with the export control and sanctions laws that apply to the information it receives and shall not export any technical data in breach of those laws.

4. Notices. Any notice under this Agreement shall be in writing and delivered by hand, by registered post or by email to the address most recently notified by the receiving party for that purpose. 5. Unauthorised disclosure. The Receiving Party has no obligation to inform the Disclosing Party of any unauthorised use or disclosure that it discovers, but it shall take reasonable steps to stop it.

6. Insurance. Each party shall maintain the insurance that is customary for a business of its size and shall provide evidence of it on reasonable request.

7. Marking of materials. The Disclosing Party may, but is not required to, add a legend to documents it provides; the absence of a legend does not by itself affect any right of either party.

8. Permitted use. The Receiving Party shall use the Confidential Information solely for the Purpose and for no other purpose.

9. Disclosure to personnel. The Receiving Party may disclose Confidential Information only to those of its employees, officers and professional advisers who need to know it for the Purpose and who are bound by written confidentiality obligations no less protective than this Agreement. It shall not disclose Confidential Information to any other person without the prior written consent of the Disclosing Party.

10. Force majeure. Neither party is liable for a delay in performing its obligations to the extent that the delay is caused by events beyond its reasonable control, provided that it gives prompt notice to the other party.

11. Public announcements. Neither party shall make a public announcement about the existence or content of the discussions between the parties without the prior written approval of the other.

12. Language. This Agreement is made in English. Any translation is for convenience only.

13. Term and termination. Either party may terminate this Agreement at any time by giving the other party thirty (30) days' written notice.

14. Assignment. Either party may assign this Agreement to a successor in connection with a merger, an acquisition or a sale of all or substantially all of its assets without the consent of the other party.

15. Reverse engineering. The Receiving Party shall not reverse engineer, disassemble or decompile any prototype, software or other tangible object that embodies Confidential Information.

16. Governing law and disputes. This Agreement shall be governed by the laws of the State of California. Any dispute arising out of it shall be finally settled by arbitration seated in San Francisco, and the courts shall not decide such disputes except to enforce an arbitral award.

18. Remedies. The sole and exclusive remedy of the Disclosing Party for any breach of this Agreement shall be monetary damages; neither party may seek injunctive or other equitable relief.

19. Non-solicitation. Nothing in this Agreement restricts either party from soliciting or hiring any employee of the other party.

A volunteer group had three jobs to fill, and three helpers, Zainab, Leila and Wei, each of whom would take exactly one. The jobs were preparing and giving the final presentation (done in the main hall); painting and building the set (done in the main hall); running the field survey in the mountains (done in the back room). The organiser wanted the allocation that used everyone's strengths and avoided friction.

Zainab had a sharp sense of humour that not everyone appreciated. Zainab read slides word for word in a monotone that put people to sleep. Zainab was handy with a drill but had never worked on anything visual. Zainab had done fieldwork in remote areas and enjoyed long days outdoors. The window was open and a cool breeze kept turning the pages of a nearby notice.

Leila lived alone, kept long hours and was known for bringing home-baked biscuits to meetings. Leila had done fieldwork in remote areas and enjoyed long days outdoors. Leila was a gifted communicator and had won the department's speaking prize. Leila had trained as a carpenter and enjoyed turning a bare stage into a believable room. A colleague who was not involved passed through twice, whistling.

Wei had been with the organisation for 4 years and was generally regarded as reliable, if a little reserved. Wei had done fieldwork in remote areas and enjoyed long days outdoors. Wei stammered under pressure and had asked never to present again. Wei had won a regional prize for stage murals and could build flats and paint them in a weekend. Meanwhile, a delivery of boxes was stacked by the door and everyone had to step around it.

Wei and Zainab had fallen out badly some months earlier, and neither would agree to work in the same room as the other for any length of time. Nobody else had any difficulty with anybody.

question.instructions:
Using the signal checklist below, rate the churn-risk level for this conversation based ONLY on the signals present in the customer's own words.

CHECKLIST:
- Explicit cancellation intent
- Competitor mention
- Deadline ultimatum
- Repeated unresolved issue (>=2 occurrences)
- Executive escalation
- Contract-end mention

LEVELS:
0: no checklist signals present
1: one signal present
2: two signals present
3: three or more signals, or explicit cancellation with a date

Rules:
- Count only distinct signals present in the customer's messages, not the agent's.
- A deadline ultimatum is present when the customer sets a specific deadline and implies or states they will disengage if the condition is not met. Polite phrasing such as 'by Friday I need an answer or we move on' still qualifies.
- 'Repeated unresolved issue (>=2)' is present when the customer explicitly states they have reported or dealt with the same problem at least twice.
- 'Executive escalation' is present when the customer mentions involving a lawyer, attorney, or other party outside the standard support chain.
- 'Contract-end mention' is present when the customer references the expiration date of their agreement or contract in the context of whether to continue.
- Do NOT count the agent's confirmation of prior tickets as the customer's statement; the customer must have explicitly referenced the repetition.
- Code-switching or mixed-language phrases do not affect signal counting; evaluate the meaning regardless of language mix.
criteria: 3: three or more signals, or explicit cancellation with a date

semantics: Events are processed strictly in the listed order. After an event, the rules that match it fire in ascending rule number, and each action is applied immediately.
A rule with a condition fires only if the condition holds at that moment; a rule marked "once" fires only the first time its trigger and condition match.

A direct user command sets the device and puts it on manual hold. Automation actions on a held device are skipped until the next "mode" event, which releases all holds before its rules fire. Commands do not trigger rules by themselves.
A lock cannot be set to locked while its door sensor reads open: the action is ignored (the lock keeps its value, and no change happens). Unlocking is always possible.
Thermostat setpoints (heat devices) are limited to the range 16-26: a larger or smaller value is stored as the nearest limit.

# Platform Moderation Policy: Targeted Harassment

**Effective Date:** 2023-01-15  
**Policy ID:** T&S-447  
**Version:** 3.2  
**Applicable Domains:** App Store reviews, developer forums, support tickets  

---

## Section 4.7: Targeted Harassment Definition

A message constitutes **targeted harassment** if and only if **ALL** of the following elements are present:

1. **Identifiable Target**: The message references a specific person who is identifiable by name, username, role, or unique descriptor.
2. **Directed Communication**: The message is clearly addressed to or about that specific person (not general complaining).
3. **Qualifying Content**: The message contains:
   - Demeaning language (insults about intelligence, appearance, character)
   - Threats of harm (physical, professional, reputational)
   - Repeated unwanted contact after a clear "stop" signal

**Exclusions** (message is NOT targeted harassment if ANY apply):

- **Public Conduct Criticism**: Critique of public actions of public figures or developers (e.g., "Your app's privacy policy is misleading").
- **Quoted Material**: Verbatim reproduction of another user's words for reporting purposes.
- **Mutual Banter**: Playful insults between users with established mutual positive interaction history (10+ helpful votes exchanged).
- **Third-Party References**: Insults directed at entities not on platform (e.g., "My boss is an idiot" when boss isn't a user).

**Implementation Notes:**  
For app reviews, the "developer" is considered a public figure for their app's conduct.  
Exclusions override primary criteria when applicable.

state.story:
The Ledger in the Storeroom

The neighbourhood association had gathered to consider its budget, but the figures on the table soon became secondary. By the time Inspector Vale arrived, the association chair lay injured in the committee room, and the meeting had become a scene requiring careful attention.

The chair was alive, though badly hurt. A metal pruning saw from the association’s locked storeroom had been used to strike them. The inspector asked everyone to remain in the building while she took statements and checked the rooms. No one disputed that the chair had been found beside the budget papers; no one could say with certainty what had happened in the minutes before the discovery.

The association secretary described the meeting’s ordinary business: repairs to the common hall, upkeep of the planted beds, and a request to replace worn tools. The chair had insisted that the accounts be reviewed openly. During the discussion, an envelope was found missing from the table. It turned up later beneath a stack of agendas, still sealed. The secretary said it contained nothing connected to the assault. A light in the corridor had also flickered, but the caretaker attributed that to a loose fitting, and the inspector found no sign that it had affected the storeroom lock.

Kofi Mensah had stayed behind after the chair asked him about private information circulating among residents. In a quiet interview, Kofi acknowledged that he had recently learned the chair was passing along his confidential affairs. He had regarded the discovery as a serious betrayal. The association’s maintenance log showed that Kofi had received instruction in using the pruning saw and other equipment kept in the storeroom. A neighbour who had stepped out into the corridor during the critical half hour said they saw Kofi by himself near the committee room. The neighbour could not say what he had been doing, but was certain no one was beside him at that moment.

Dana Whitlock’s statement was composed and detailed. Dana said the chair’s absence would bring no advantage: there was no dispute over money, a position, or any decision that could benefit Dana if the chair were gone. The maintenance log also recorded Dana’s instruction in the safe use of the association’s tools, including the pruning saw. When the inspector asked about the critical half hour, Dana could not produce anyone who had remained with them or could confirm their whereabouts. Dana said they had been moving between the hall and the entrance, but no witness could place them there throughout that period.

Henrik Dahl had attended to speak about the planted beds and had no quarrel with the chair, according to both his own account and the secretary’s notes. The inspector found nothing to suggest that the chair’s absence would have brought Henrik any gain. The storeroom register and the caretaker’s account agreed that Henrik had never been given access to that room and did not possess a key. A resident recalled seeing Henrik alone near the committee room during the critical half hour. Henrik said he had been looking for a copy of the planting plan, which was later found in the hall.

The inspector checked the pruning saw for damage and confirmed that it belonged in the storeroom. The key register showed no unexplained entry, and the caretaker said the room had been secured before the meeting. She cautioned the association members against turning every awkward detail into evidence: the misplaced envelope, the flickering corridor light, and the planting plan explained nothing about the attack. The statements and records, she said, were more useful when considered together than when treated as isolated suspicions.

As the meeting room emptied, the inspector left the budget papers untouched and reviewed the three accounts once more. The chair’s injury had made the unresolved personal tensions impossible to ignore, but the decision before the association was not about who seemed most resentful or who had offered the strangest explanation. It depended on what the testimony and records established about the person responsible.

Notice from the highways department of the borough council: Ashford Gardens resurfacing. Work is due to begin on 19 February. Completion is planned after 5 weeks. Residents with questions can write to the highways department or attend the drop-in session at the library. Alder Building Services has been appointed to carry out the works. 13 parking bays will be suspended during the works. The project has a budget of £515,000. The same stretch was last resurfaced 11 years ago, and the cycle lane was added at that time. The road will be closed to traffic from 7 am to 6 pm on working days. A separate project on a nearby road starts on 24 February. The previous resurfacing nearby was carried out by Alder Civil Engineering. A signed diversion runs along Cedar Bridge. Waste collection will take place as usual, although bins on the closed section should be left at the nearest junction. Pedestrian access to shops will be maintained throughout, and temporary crossings will be marked with yellow signs.

Notice from the highways department of the borough council: Northgate Road resurfacing. Work is due to begin on 13 May. During the works, 26 parking bays will be unavailable. Marlow Building Services has been appointed to carry out the works. Waste collection will take place as usual, although bins on the closed section should be left at the nearest junction. The works are expected to last 7 weeks. The same stretch was last resurfaced 11 years ago, and the cycle lane was added at that time. The road will be closed to traffic from 8 am to 5 pm on working days. Residents with questions can write to the highways department or attend the drop-in session at the library. A signed diversion runs along Eastley Park. The total cost is estimated at £210,000. The council says it has consulted residents’ associations and local businesses on the timing of the works. Last year the council spent £220,000 on resurfacing a neighbouring street.

state.problem: We renewed the certificate on the load balancer last week and monitoring says all is well, but customers on our older point-of-sale terminals say they get a certificate warning for the domain, while modern devices are fine. The servers host several sites. What could cause a name mismatch for old devices only?
documents: D1. Key Rotation and the JWKS Endpoint: Issuers publish signing keys at a JWKS address and rotate them periodically. A validator that caches the key set forever starts rejecting every new token after rotation. Cache with an expiry and refetch when an unknown key id appears.

D2. Mutual TLS: In mutual TLS the client also presents a certificate that the server validates against its own trust list. Failures usually show up as handshake errors on the server side, and the usual causes are an expired client certificate, a missing intermediate or a client certificate issued by an authority the server does not trust.

D3. Consumer Group Rebalancing: When consumers join or leave a group, partitions are redistributed. During a rebalance processing pauses, and messages handled but not yet committed may be processed again by the new owner. Long processing between polls can make the broker think a consumer died and trigger rebalances.

D4. SNI and Multiple Sites on One IP: Server Name Indication lets the client announce the hostname during the handshake so that the server presents the matching certificate. Old clients without SNI receive the server's default certificate, which may not match, producing a name mismatch only for them.

D5. Implicit Rounding With Formats: Number formats change only the display. A column showing two decimals still sums its full precision values, so visible numbers may not add up to the displayed total by a cent. Use ROUND in the formula if the displayed values must add up.

D6. Message Size Limits: Brokers cap message size, often around 1 MB. Large payloads should be stored elsewhere (object storage) and the message should carry a reference. Oversized messages are rejected at the producer or cause timeouts.

D7. Self-Signed and Private CAs: A certificate signed by a private authority is trusted only on machines whose trust store contains that authority's root. Disabling verification to make it work removes protection against interception. Distribute the root through device management or pin it for the specific client.

D8. Hostname Matching: A client checks that the server name it connected to appears in the certificate's subject alternative names. A certificate for example.com does not cover www.example.com or api.example.com unless listed or covered by a wildcard, and a wildcard covers only one label.

D9. Clock Errors Look Like Certificate Errors: If a device's clock is wrong, a perfectly valid certificate may appear 'not yet valid' or 'expired'. Embedded devices that boot without a battery-backed clock before they sync time are typical. Check the system date before debugging the certificate.

D10. Revocation Checking: Certificates can be revoked before expiry, but clients check revocation via lists or OCSP, which can fail open or be slow. OCSP stapling lets the server attach a signed recent status to the handshake, avoiding extra lookups for the client.

D11. Array and Spill Behaviour: Modern spreadsheets let one formula return many values that spill into neighbouring cells. If the cells below are not empty the formula shows a spill error. Older versions require entering such formulas as array formulas.

D12. Merged Cells and Sorting: Merged cells break sorting, filtering and many formulas because they occupy several grid cells while only one holds the value. Use Center Across Selection or restructure the table so every row has its own cells.

D13. Retention and Replay: A log keeps messages for a retention period or size regardless of consumption. A new consumer can start from the beginning to rebuild state, but only as far back as retention allows. Compacted topics keep the latest value per key instead.

D14. Certificate Chain Completeness: A server must send its certificate plus the intermediate certificates that link it to a trusted root. Browsers sometimes fetch missing intermediates, but many clients, scripts and mobile libraries do not and report 'unable to get local issuer certificate'. Install the full chain on the server.

D15. Authorization Code With PKCE: Public clients such as mobile apps cannot keep a secret. In the code flow they generate a random verifier, send its hash in the authorization request, and prove possession of the verifier when exchanging the code. An attacker who intercepts the code cannot redeem it without the verifier.

D16. Token Validation and Clock Skew: JWT validation checks the signature with the issuer's published keys, the expiry, not-before and issuer claims. Servers whose clocks differ by a minute may reject fresh tokens as not yet valid. A small leeway of a few minutes, and time sync, avoid spurious failures.

D17. Hidden Rows and Aggregates: SUBTOTAL and AGGREGATE can ignore filtered or hidden rows; SUM includes them. A total that doesn't change when you filter a table is using SUM. Conversely, a total that changes unexpectedly after hiding rows is using SUBTOTAL.

D18. Certificate Transparency: Public CAs log issued certificates in public append-only logs, and browsers may require proof of logging. Domain owners can monitor the logs to detect unexpected certificates issued for their names.

D19. Numbers Stored as Text: Cells that look like numbers but are stored as text, often after import, are ignored by SUM and sorted as text so that 100 comes before 20. A leading apostrophe, left alignment or a green corner flag hint at it. Convert with VALUE, multiplying by 1 or Text to Columns.

D20. Expiry and Renewal Automation: Certificates have a validity end date and clients reject expired ones with no grace period. Short-lived certificates renewed automatically avoid outages caused by forgotten renewals. Monitoring should alert weeks before expiry and also verify that renewed certificates are actually deployed.

D21. Key and Certificate Mismatch: A certificate must match the private key on the server. Deploying a renewed certificate with the old key (or vice versa) makes the server fail to start or the handshake fail. Comparing the public key hash of the certificate and key reveals the mismatch.

D22. ID Token Versus Access Token: An ID token tells the client who authenticated and is meant for the client; an access token is for calling APIs and its contents may be opaque to the client. Sending an ID token to an API as a bearer credential mixes the two purposes and can allow tokens issued for another client to be accepted.

D23. Leading Zeros and Long Numbers: Opening a CSV converts postcodes like 01067 to the number 1067 and long identifiers like 12345678901234567 to scientific notation with lost digits beyond 15 significant digits. Import those columns as text before the conversion happens.

Northline Home’s Alder countertop mixer includes a two-year limited warranty beginning on the date of purchase. The warranty covers defects in materials and workmanship when the mixer is used in a household kitchen according to the printed instructions. It does not cover damage caused by commercial use, unauthorized repairs, or use of attachments not approved by Northline. Normal wear on the whisk coating and cosmetic scratches are also excluded.

To request service, the purchaser must contact Northline’s support desk and provide proof of purchase, the mixer’s serial number, and a description of the problem. Northline may ask the purchaser to mail the mixer to its service center; the purchaser pays the shipping cost to the center, while Northline pays return shipping for covered repairs. If Northline confirms a covered defect, it may repair the mixer or replace it with a new or refurbished unit at its discretion. The warranty does not promise a particular repair turnaround time.

The warranty applies only to the original purchaser and cannot be transferred. Purchases from authorized Northline retailers qualify, while secondhand purchases and purchases from unauthorized sellers do not. Registering the mixer online is optional and does not change the warranty period or the service process. Local consumer rights may provide additional protections, and the written warranty does not limit those rights where applicable.

The study is being conducted at the Northbank clinic and is not a test of a new medication. Researchers plan to enroll 60 adults, ages 21 to 65, who have been diagnosed with mild asthma for at least one year and live within 25 miles of the clinic. People who smoke currently or have been hospitalized for asthma in the past six months are not eligible.

Participation lasts 10 weeks. At the first clinic visit, which takes about 90 minutes, staff will review the consent form, collect a medical history, and provide a monitor for use at home. Participants will record symptoms and monitor readings in a study app each day. They will return to the clinic at weeks 4 and 10 for visits lasting about 30 minutes; the monitor will be collected at the final visit. The study does not ask participants to change their usual asthma treatment, and their regular clinician will continue to manage their care.

Participants may receive up to $180 in gift cards for completing all study activities: $60 after the first visit, $40 after the week-4 visit, and $80 after the final visit. Travel costs are not reimbursed. Enrollment is open through March 31, 2027, or until all 60 places are filled. state.policy:
Travel and Expense Policy. This policy governs reimbursement of business-trip expenses for employees. Amounts are in euros.
1. Definitions. A "business trip" is a trip with at least one overnight stay away from the employee's home city that has been approved in advance. A "travel day" is any calendar day from the day of departure to the day of return, both included. "Grade" is the employee's grade from 1 to 4 as shown on the claim. City class A, B or C is assigned to the destination in Annex 1.
2. Hotel. The hotel is reimbursed per night up to the cap for the city class and grade (euros per night): class A: 160 (grades 1-2) / 185 (grades 3-4); class B: 120 (grades 1-2) / 135 (grades 3-4); class C: 95 (grades 1-2) / 115 (grades 3-4). Amounts above the cap are not reimbursed; the cap applies to every night.
3. Meals. Meals are reimbursed as a flat allowance of 48 euros per travel day. On the first and the last travel day the allowance is 50 % of that amount. For each meal that was provided free of charge (for example at a conference), the allowance of that travel day is reduced by 20 % of the full daily amount for breakfast and 30 % for lunch or dinner; the allowance of a day never falls below zero. No receipts are needed for the allowance.
4. Flights. Flights are reimbursed at the economy fare. Business class is reimbursed in full only if the flight lasts more than 7 hours and the employee is grade 3 or higher; otherwise the reimbursement is limited to the economy fare that the claim states for the same flight.
5. Local transport. Public transport and taxis at the destination are reimbursed up to 20 euros per travel day in total. Items of more than 25 euros need an original receipt. Items of up to 25 euros without a receipt are reimbursed only if those items together do not exceed 75 euros; otherwise none of them is reimbursed.
6. Excluded items. Alcoholic drinks, minibar, personal entertainment and leisure, spa and fitness, parking fines and any other fines are never reimbursed, even if they appear on a hotel invoice.

TENANCY DEPOSIT RETURN SCHEME FOR LEASED PREMISES
Issued by CivicSure Deposits Ltd.


1. DEFINITIONS AND GENERAL TERMS
  1.1 To initiate a request, the tenant must contact the dedicated deposit support team by email or postal address provided in the scheme documentation. The request must include the tenancy reference number and the date the tenancy ended, and must be accompanied by the required document listed above.
  1.2 All personal data submitted as part of a deposit return request is processed solely for the administration of this scheme. Data is held securely and is not shared with third parties except where required for legal compliance, dispute resolution, or the legitimate handling of the tenancy. Retention periods follow industry standards.
  1.3 If any clause in this policy is found to be unenforceable or invalid, the remainder of the policy shall continue in full force and effect. This policy is governed by the law applicable to the tenancy's jurisdiction, and the provider's decisions are made in accordance with that law and the principles of fairness and transparency.

2. COVERAGE AND LIMITS
  2.1 The scheme covers the following categories:
  - Full Deposit Return: Covers the return of the entire deposit when the tenancy ends with no unpaid rent and no damage beyond fair wear and tear. Per-claim limit: £800.
  - Partial Deposit Return: Covers the return of a portion of the deposit after agreed deductions for specific, evidenced costs such as cleaning, repairs, or unpaid bills. Per-claim limit: £250.
  - Deduction Dispute: Covers a request to challenge deductions proposed by the landlord, where the tenant believes the deduction is unjustified or over‑stated. Per-claim limit: £3,000.
  - Guarantor Refund: Covers the return of deposit funds to a guarantor who paid the deposit on behalf of the tenant, when the tenancy ends with no outstanding obligations. Per-claim limit: £2,500.
  2.2 The per-claim limit is applied to the loss first; the deductible of £150 is then subtracted from the capped amount.
  2.3 The tenant bears no co-payment.
  2.4 Total payments in one policy year may not exceed £8,000; amounts already paid in the year reduce what remains.

3. EXCLUSIONS
  3.1 No deposit return will be made if the tenant vacates the premises without notice and leaves belongings or unpaid rent, as determined by the landlord's inventory and final inspection.
  3.2 No deposit return is due if the tenant kept a pet on the premises without written consent from the landlord, and the pet caused damage or excessive cleaning costs.
  3.3 The deposit will not be returned if smoking occurred inside the premises and this resulted in residual odour or yellowing of walls or fabrics that require professional remediation.
  3.4 If rent remains unpaid at the end of the tenancy, the deposit is withheld entirely until the arrears are settled, and no partial return is processed.

4. CONDITIONS
  4.1 Nothing is payable for a loss occurring fewer than 30 days after the inception date.
  4.2 A deposit return request must be notified within 30 days after the loss date; later notification is not accepted.
  4.3 Every deposit return request must be accompanied by the final signed inventory and check‑out inspection report.

5. ASSESSMENT PROCEDURE
  Each deposit return request is assessed in this order and the first applicable step decides it: (a) waiting period (4.1), (b) notification deadline (4.2), (c) exclusions (Section 3; the lowest-numbered applicable exclusion is named), (d) documentation (4.3: the deposit return request is held, not denied), (e) amount (Section 2), (f) any amount above £2,000 requires senior-adjuster sign-off before payment.

6. PRECEDENCE
  If any other part of these terms conflicts with Section 3 or Section 5, Sections 3 and 5 prevail.
  This scheme applies to all tenancy deposits held by CivicSure Deposits Ltd. for residential leases of one year or longer. The tenant named on the tenancy agreement, or their authorised guarantor, is the only person entitled to make a request under this policy.

7. ADMINISTRATION
  7.1 CivicSure Deposits Ltd. will process the deposit return in accordance with the terms of the original tenancy agreement and any applicable law on deposit protection. The provider may request additional clarification or evidence from the tenant or the landlord to verify the validity of the request.
  7.2 If the tenant disagrees with an outcome, they may raise an objection in writing to the provider's disputes team within a reasonable period after receiving the decision. The provider will acknowledge the complaint and aim to investigate fairly, giving the tenant the opportunity to provide further evidence.

state.story:
Ticket ID: TB-4187. The first call reached the telecom billing helpdesk while the night shift was still sorting disputed roaming charges. A supervisor had been found unconscious in the locked storeroom, and the company’s sealed backup handset was missing from its charging cradle. The handset held a test account used to verify billing adjustments, so the incident had already become more than an ordinary workplace assault. Detective Vale arrived as staff were being asked to stay put and keep their hands off the terminals.

The storeroom door had not been forced. Its key opened the room, and the access log showed no useful entry because the lock was old and did not record openings. Vale asked each employee where they had been during the critical half hour. The victim was alive when last seen heading toward the storeroom; later, a cleaner found them on the floor. The medic said the injury was serious, but the victim could not yet give a statement. No one could say whether the missing handset had been the reason for the attack or merely an opportunity that presented itself.

Greta Vogel gave a brisk account while keeping one eye on the ringing helpdesk line. A stockroom register confirmed that she had a key to the locked storeroom where the handset was kept. A colleague had seen Greta by herself near the scene during the critical half hour. When Vale asked what she might gain if the victim were absent, Greta said nothing, and the billing manager’s records backed that up: the victim’s absence brought Greta no advantage. Her name appeared on a separate complaint about a customer’s disputed charge, but the complaint had been resolved and did not connect her to the storeroom.

Owen Pritchard’s reason for resenting the victim was less obscure. The victim’s share of the business was due to pass to Owen, according to a document the company’s solicitor had verified. Yet the access administrator showed Vale a deactivation receipt: Owen had returned their entry code a week earlier. A building guard also remembered Owen leaving before the critical half hour began. Owen claimed he had gone home to settle an argument over an unpaid phone bill, a detail that sounded dramatic but led nowhere; the account belonged to a relative and had no bearing on the missing handset.

Priya Raman had her own grievance. She had been passed over for promotion, and the position had gone to the victim. The decision appeared in the staffing file, along with Priya’s written appeal. Still, the access administrator’s record showed that Priya, like Owen, had turned in her code a week earlier. That did not place her beyond the building: two helpdesk agents saw her alone near the storeroom during the critical half hour. Priya said she had been looking for a dropped headset. A headset was later found beneath a desk in the billing bay, but nothing established that it belonged to her, and the discovery did not explain the attack.

Henrik Dahl had arrived to press the victim about money. A ledger and a series of unanswered messages showed that the victim owed him a large sum. Henrik also had a key to the locked storeroom where the handset had been kept; the facilities clerk recognized the key on his ring and confirmed it still worked. Vale checked who might account for Henrik during the critical half hour. No one could vouch for his whereabouts then. Henrik said he had been walking between the service corridor and the loading area, but the corridor camera was out of order and the loading door showed no reliable record of who passed through.

Vale returned to the helpdesk floor. The agents were still taking calls, their voices lowered as they explained billing holds to customers who had no idea a crime scene sat behind the office doors. The incident log, access paperwork, staffing records, and witness accounts did not all point in the same direction. Some details were motives without a route into the locked room; other details placed people nearby without granting them access or a personal stake. Vale set the statements beside the storeroom key register and waited for the medic to report whether the victim could speak.

You are the investigator who must make the next call: which suspect should be identified as the culprit, based on the evidence?

CYPHERSHIELD INSURANCE POLICY - SCHEDULE OF COVERAGES
SECTION 7: DATA BREACH LIABILITY

7.1 DEFINITIONS
A 'Security Incident' is defined as the unauthorized access, acquisition, or disclosure of Non-Public Personal Information (NPI).

7.2 EXCLUSIONS
This policy does not cover:
a) Losses resulting from the failure of the Insured to implement security measures recommended in the previous annual audit, provided such measures were listed in the 'Mandatory' category.
b) Any claim where the Insured admits to intentional omission of security controls after a known vulnerability scan.

7.3 CLAIMS PROCESSING & TRIAGE
In the event of a reported breach, the claims administrator shall review the First Notice of Loss (FNOL) against the following Red-Flag Checklist:

FLAG A: 'Ghost' Data. The breach report cites data categories not explicitly listed in the Policy Schedule of Data Types.
FLAG B: Delayed Notification. The Insured notifies the carrier more than 72 hours after becoming aware of the incident.
FLAG C: Vendor Involvement. The breach originates from a third-party vendor not listed in the Approved Vendor List.
FLAG D: 'Critical' Flag - Systemic Failure. The breach affects 100% of the Insured's customer database or involves the main production server credentials.

REFERRAL RULE: A claim is referred to the Special Investigations Unit (SIU) if 3 or more flags are met, OR if the 'Critical' Flag (Flag D) is met.

---

Insured: DataFlow Inc.

Breach Type: Phishing email leading to credential theft.

Database Impact: The breach compromised 15,000 out of 50,000 customer records. The main production server credentials were NOT compromised; only a single user account was targeted.

state.problem: I added a fixed bar to the top of my page and gave the first heading a top margin of 30px. The whole content block, including its background, shifted down by 30px instead of the heading moving inside the block. There is no padding or border on the block. Why does the margin escape?
documents: D1. Selectivity and When Scans Win: An index helps when it narrows the result to a small fraction of rows. For a column where 90% of rows share the same value, a sequential scan is cheaper than jumping through the index for most of the table, so the planner ignores the index. A partial index covering only the rare value can be useful.

D2. Floats and Collapsed Parents: A parent that contains only floated children has zero height because floats are taken out of normal flow, so backgrounds and borders of the parent do not wrap them. Clearing the float, or giving the parent display: flow-root, makes it contain its floats.

D3. Inline Elements and Vertical Space: Inline elements such as images sit on the text baseline, which leaves a gap below them for descenders. A few pixels of unexplained space under an image inside a container comes from that. Setting display: block or vertical-align: middle on the image removes the gap.

D4. Collation and Case-Insensitive Matching: Comparisons use the column's collation, which defines the sort order and whether 'a' equals 'A'. An index built with one collation cannot serve queries that require another, and a case-insensitive search against a case-sensitive index falls back to scanning. Choose the collation when creating the column.

D5. Overflow and Sticky Positioning: position: sticky only works relative to its nearest scrolling ancestor. If a parent between the element and the page has overflow set to hidden, auto or scroll, the element sticks to that parent instead of the viewport, and may seem not to stick at all. Also the sticky element needs a threshold such as top: 0.

D6. Stacking Contexts and z-index: z-index only compares elements within the same stacking context. A child with z-index 9999 inside a parent that creates its own stacking context (for example through opacity below 1, transform, or position with z-index) can never appear above a sibling of that parent that has a higher z-index. Fix the structure, not the number.

D7. Write Amplification From Many Indexes: Every insert or update must modify each index that contains an affected column. A table with fifteen indexes can have write throughput several times lower than the same table with three. Dropping unused indexes found through usage statistics speeds up writes and reduces storage.

D8. Caching Personalised Responses: A response containing user-specific data must not be stored under a shared key or in a shared HTTP cache. Either vary the key by user or segment, or cache the common part and add personal data afterward. Mistakes here leak data between accounts.

D9. Unsafe Publication: Making an object reachable to other threads before its constructor finishes, for example by storing this in a static field inside the constructor, may expose partially initialised fields. Final fields get special guarantees; otherwise publish through a volatile reference, a lock or a concurrent collection.

D10. Offset Pagination Cost: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000 must still produce and discard the first 100,000 rows in the sort order, so later pages are slower than early ones. Keyset pagination, filtering on the last seen sort key with a matching index, reads only the next 20 rows.

D11. Non-Thread-Safe Library Classes: Classes such as SimpleDateFormat and ArrayList are not safe for concurrent use. Sharing one formatter between request threads yields garbled dates or exceptions that appear only under load. Use thread-confined instances, ThreadLocal, or immutable alternatives like DateTimeFormatter.

D12. Grid Auto Placement and Gaps: In a CSS grid, items are placed in the next free cell in order. An item spanning several columns can leave holes that later items do not fill, unless grid-auto-flow: dense is set. Gaps are spacing between tracks only, not around the outer edge, which surprises people expecting equal margins.

D13. Positioned Elements and Containing Blocks: A position: absolute element is placed relative to the nearest ancestor that is itself positioned (not static). If none exists, it is placed relative to the page. Forgetting position: relative on the intended parent makes the child jump to a far corner.

D14. Margin Collapsing: Vertical margins of adjacent block elements, or of a parent and its first or last child with no padding or border between them, combine into the larger of the two instead of adding. A child's top margin can therefore appear to push the parent down. Padding, a border, or establishing a new formatting context stops it.

D15. Flex Items Shrinking and min-width: Flex items default to min-width: auto, which prevents them from shrinking below the size of their content. A long unbroken string or wide image can make a flex child overflow its container. Setting min-width: 0 on the item, or overflow: hidden, lets it shrink.

D16. Write-Through Versus Write-Back: Write-through writes to the cache and the database synchronously, keeping them consistent at the cost of write latency. Write-back acknowledges after the cache write and flushes to the database later, which is faster but risks losing acknowledged writes if the cache node fails before flushing.

D17. Serialisation Cost: Storing large objects in a cache requires serialising and deserialising them on every access. For big structures this CPU time can exceed the database query it replaces. Caching a smaller derived result, or only the fields needed, keeps the benefit.

D18. Thread Pool Starvation: In a fixed-size pool, tasks that block waiting for other tasks submitted to the same pool can occupy all threads, leaving none to run the awaited tasks. The pool deadlocks without any lock being involved. Use separate pools for dependent work or non-blocking composition.

D19. Covering Indexes and Index-Only Scans: When every column a query reads is included in the index, the engine can answer from the index alone without visiting the table rows. Including extra non-key columns for this purpose speeds up read-heavy reports, but each added column makes the index larger and slows writes. Visibility information may still force some table visits.

D20. Implicit Type Conversion: If a column is stored as text and a query compares it with a number, or the reverse, the database may convert every row's value before comparing, which defeats the index. The comparison also may behave differently from what you expect, for example '10' sorting before '9'. Match the literal's type to the column's type.

Finally, the team fixed a bug that could leave a completed task visible in the “Assigned to me” list until the user refreshed the page. The fix applies to both web and mobile clients. EMPLOYER-SPONSORED OUTPATIENT AND EMERGENCY MEDICAL COST REIMBURSEMENT SCHEME
Issued by MediReturn Administrative Services Ltd.


1. DEFINITIONS AND GENERAL TERMS
  1.1 We process personal data in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation. Your medical and financial information is used solely for assessing and paying your reimbursement request and is shared only with the employer and relevant service providers as necessary. We retain records for the duration required by law.
  1.2 If any provision of this scheme is found to be invalid or unenforceable by a court of competent jurisdiction, the remaining provisions shall remain in full force and effect. This scheme represents the entire agreement regarding the reimbursement of medical costs and supersedes any prior verbal or written agreements.
  1.3 If you are dissatisfied with the outcome of your request, you may submit a complaint in writing to our compliance office. We will review your case and provide a written response. Complaints must include your full name, the request reference number, and a clear description of the issue.

2. COVERAGE AND LIMITS
  2.1 The scheme covers the following categories:
  - Primary Care Visits: Covers consultations with general practitioners, pediatricians, and other primary care physicians for diagnosis and treatment of acute conditions. Per-event limit: €400.
  - Prescription Medications: Covers the cost of medications prescribed by a licensed healthcare provider for the treatment of a covered condition. Per-event limit: €5,000.
  - Diagnostic Laboratory Tests: Covers blood tests, urine tests, and other laboratory analyses ordered by a physician to diagnose or monitor a medical condition. Per-event limit: €2,500.
  - Emergency Room Treatment: Covers treatment received at a hospital emergency department for a sudden, severe, or life-threatening condition, including stabilization and initial care. Per-event limit: €400.
  2.2 The per-event limit is applied to the loss first; the deductible of €100 is then subtracted from the capped amount.
  2.3 The employee bears 10% of the amount remaining after the deductible and limit; the provider pays the rest.
  2.4 Total payments in one policy year may not exceed €20,000; amounts already paid in the year reduce what remains.

3. EXCLUSIONS
  3.1 Any procedure performed primarily for aesthetic purposes, including but not limited to cosmetic surgery, laser resurfacing, or liposuction, is excluded unless medically necessary to restore function or treat an injury.
  3.2 Medications that are available without a prescription, such as pain relievers, antihistamines, or vitamins, are excluded from reimbursement even if recommended by a physician.
  3.3 Routine dental check-ups, cleanings, fillings, extractions, and routine eye exams or corrective lenses are excluded, unless required due to an accidental injury or a covered illness.
  3.4 Medical services received outside the European Economic Area (EEA) are excluded, except in cases of emergency care required during business travel.

4. CONDITIONS
  4.1 Nothing is payable for a loss occurring fewer than 7 days after the inception date.
  4.2 A reimbursement request must be notified within 30 days after the loss date; later notification is not accepted.
  4.3 Every reimbursement request must be accompanied by the itemized invoice from the healthcare provider.

5. ASSESSMENT PROCEDURE
  Each reimbursement request is assessed in this order and the first applicable step decides it: (a) waiting period (4.1), (b) notification deadline (4.2), (c) exclusions (Section 3; the lowest-numbered applicable exclusion is named), (d) documentation (4.3: the reimbursement request is held, not denied), (e) amount (Section 2), (f) any amount above €1,200 requires senior-adjuster sign-off before payment.

6. PRECEDENCE
  If any other part of these terms conflicts with Section 3 or Section 5, Sections 3 and 5 prevail.
  In this scheme, 'you' refers to the employee who is eligible under the terms of your employment contract. 'We' or 'us' refers to MediReturn Administrative Services Ltd., acting on behalf of your employer. The scheme is governed by the rules set out in this document and the corresponding employer policy.

7. ADMINISTRATION
  7.1 To submit a reimbursement request, you must complete the online form available on the employee portal. You must attach the required documentation as specified in the scheme description, and you must provide your personal identification number and bank account details for payment.
  7.2 If you have questions about this scheme, you may contact our support team by email at support@medireturn.example or by telephone at the number printed on your employee benefits card. Our operating hours are from nine in the morning to five in the afternoon, Monday through Friday.

state.problem: Our mobile app lets users log in with a standard OAuth flow. After a successful login, we store the access token and the refresh token in the app's secure storage. When the access token expires, we try to refresh. But sometimes, the refresh call fails with -invalid_grant-. We have seen that if we quickly press 'refresh' twice in a row, the second attempt always fails. We are not sure if it is our code or the server. How should we handle this to avoid breaking the user's session?
documents: D1. Resource Server Access Token Validation: A resource server must validate any incoming access token before serving data. If the token is a JWT, it can validate locally by checking the signature with the issuer's public key, the expiration, the audience claim, and the issuer. If the token is opaque, it must call the introspection endpoint. The resource server should also check the required scope for the specific resource. If validation fails, return 401 Unauthorized with a WWW-Authenticate header indicating the error. Do not attempt to decode the token's payload without proper validation, as that is a security risk.

D2. JWT Claims for User Identification: A JWT commonly contains claims like sub for the user identifier, email, name, and perhaps groups or roles. The sub claim is immutable and globally unique within the issuer. Never use email as the primary identifier because it can change. The resource server should extract the user identity from the sub claim after verifying the signature and audience. The token may also contain session or nonce claims for state. Ensure you do not trust the claims without verification. The exact set of claims is defined by the issuer and documented in its discovery endpoint.

D3. JWT Structure and Signature Validation: A JSON Web Token (JWT) has three parts: header, payload, and signature, each base64url-encoded and separated by dots. The header declares the algorithm, e.g., RS256, and the key ID. The payload contains claims like iss, sub, exp, and custom scopes. The signature is computed over the header and payload using the specified algorithm and a private key. Validators must fetch the public key from the issuer's JWKS endpoint and verify the signature. They must also check the exp, nbf, and aud claims. Do not trust a JWT without verifying its signature, and reject tokens with mismatched algorithms or missing required claims.

D4. Scopes and Scope Validation: Scopes are space-delimited strings that define the specific permissions an access token grants. They are requested by the client during authorization, and the server may grant a subset. A resource server must check that the access token's scope includes the required permission before serving a protected resource. If the token lacks a scope, the server returns 403 Forbidden with an insufficient_scope error. Scopes are not hierarchical unless explicitly designed, so read and write are separate. Clients should request the least permissive set of scopes needed, and users must consent to them during the authorization step.

D5. Client Credentials Grant for Machine-to-Machine: The client credentials grant is used when a confidential client acts on its own behalf, not on behalf of a user. The client authenticates to the token endpoint using its client secret or private key and receives an access token with scopes that reflect its own permissions. There is no refresh token because the client can always obtain a new token by re-authenticating. This grant is typical for server-to-server APIs, cron jobs, and background services. The token should be stored securely and short-lived. The client credentials must never be exposed in browser code. This flow requires no user interaction and no authorization endpoint.

D6. Introspection Endpoint: The token introspection endpoint allows a resource server to query the authorization server about the current state of an access token. The resource server sends a POST with the token value and its own client credentials. The response includes active (true or false), plus metadata like scope, client_id, username, and expiration time. If a token has been revoked or has expired, active is false. Introspection is useful when the resource server cannot validate JWT signatures directly or needs real-time revocation status. It incurs a network round trip per request, so caching the result for a short time is common.

D7. Access Token Expiration and Refresh Flow: Access tokens are short-lived credentials, typically valid for minutes to a few hours, to limit blast radius if leaked. When an access token expires, the client must use a refresh token to obtain a new access token. The refresh token is long-lived and stored securely, usually server-side or in a secure device enclave. The refresh request is a POST to the token endpoint with grant_type=refresh_token and the refresh token value. The authorization server may rotate refresh tokens, invalidating the old one after each use. Clients must handle the -invalid_grant- response by re-authenticating the user, not by blindly retrying.

D8. Revocation of Tokens: The revocation endpoint allows a client to invalidate a refresh token or access token. The client POSTs the token and its type (refresh_token or access_token) to the revocation endpoint. The authorization server marks the token as invalid; subsequent use fails with -invalid_token-. Revocation is crucial for security when a device is lost or a user logs out. The client must also delete its local copy. Revocation of a refresh token does not automatically revoke its associated access tokens, but they will expire shortly. Servers may revoke all tokens for a user or client upon password change.

D12. Refresh Token Rotation and Reuse Detection: Refresh token rotation means the authorization server issues a new refresh token with every refresh request and invalidates the old one. This prevents a stolen refresh token from being replayed. If a client attempts to use an already-used refresh token, the server detects that as a reuse and should invalidate the entire family of tokens, requiring a full re-authentication. Clients must always store the latest refresh token after each response. A typical flow: the client sends the old refresh token, receives a new one plus an access token, and atomically replaces the stored refresh token. If the refresh response fails, the client should discard the old token and ask the user to log in again.

sémantique: Les événements sont traités strictement dans l'ordre indiqué. Après un événement, les règles correspondantes se déclenchent par numéro de règle croissant et chaque action est appliquée immédiatement.

Une règle avec condition ne se déclenche que si la condition est vraie à cet instant ; une règle marquée « unique » ne se déclenche qu'à la première correspondance de son déclencheur et de sa condition.

Une commande directe de l'utilisateur règle l'appareil et le place en maintien manuel. Les actions d'automatisation sur un appareil maintenu sont ignorées jusqu'au prochain événement « mode », qui lève tous les maintiens avant le déclenchement de ses règles. Les commandes ne déclenchent pas de règles par elles-mêmes.

state.policy:
Travel and Expense Policy. This policy governs reimbursement of business-trip expenses for employees. Amounts are in euros.
1. Definitions. A "business trip" is a trip with at least one overnight stay away from the employee's home city that has been approved in advance. A "travel day" is any calendar day from the day of departure to the day of return, both included. "Grade" is the employee's grade from 1 to 4 as shown on the claim. City class A, B or C is assigned to the destination in Annex 1.
2. Hotel. The hotel is reimbursed per night up to the cap for the city class and grade (euros per night): class A: 170 (grades 1-2) / 195 (grades 3-4); class B: 120 (grades 1-2) / 140 (grades 3-4); class C: 95 (grades 1-2) / 115 (grades 3-4). Amounts above the cap are not reimbursed; the cap applies to every night.
3. Meals. Meals are reimbursed as a flat allowance of 40 euros per travel day. On the first and the last travel day the allowance is 50 % of that amount. For each meal that was provided free of charge (for example at a conference), the allowance of that travel day is reduced by 20 % of the full daily amount for breakfast and 30 % for lunch or dinner; the allowance of a day never falls below zero. No receipts are needed for the allowance.
4. Flights. Flights are reimbursed at the economy fare. Business class is reimbursed in full only if the flight lasts more than 5 hours and the employee is grade 4 or higher; otherwise the reimbursement is limited to the economy fare that the claim states for the same flight.
5. Local transport. Public transport and taxis at the destination are reimbursed up to 18 euros per travel day in total. Items of more than 20 euros need an original receipt. Items of up to 20 euros without a receipt are reimbursed only if those items together do not exceed 60 euros; otherwise none of them is reimbursed.
6. Excluded items. Alcoholic drinks, minibar, personal entertainment and leisure, spa and fitness, parking fines and any other fines are never reimbursed, even if they appear on a hotel invoice.
7. Private car. If the employee uses a private car, mileage is reimbursed at 0.30 euros per kilometre. This clause does not apply to taxis or rented cars.
8. Late claims. A claim must be submitted within 30 days after the day of return. If it is submitted later but within 75 days, the total reimbursable amount is reduced by 15 %. After 75 days the claim is rejected.
9. Approval. The approver is determined by the total reimbursable amount after all deductions: up to and including 600 euros the line manager approves; above that and up to and including 1800 euros the department head approves; above 1800 euros the finance director approves. A rejected claim needs no approval.
10. Records. Claims and receipts are kept for ten years. Personal data on receipts is processed under the company data protection notice.
Additional provisions (these do not change the numbered clauses above):
- Tips. Tips of up to 10 % of an invoice are included in the item they relate to when the item is otherwise reimbursable.
- Advance payments. Employees may request an advance of up to 70 % of the expected hotel and travel costs, at the earliest ten days before departure. Advances are settled against the claim and do not change the rules for reimbursement.
- Loyalty programmes. Points, miles and bonus credits earned on business trips may be kept by the employee. They may not be used to upgrade a booking that the company pays for.
- Trips abroad. For trips to destinations outside the home country a separate foreign-travel annex applies, with country-specific meal allowances between 55 and 95 euros per day. The annex is not part of this policy and is issued by the finance department.
Annex 1. City classes: A = capital and financial centres; B = other cities above 250,000 inhabitants; C = all other places.

Selin Haldane, curator of the Albrecht Gallery, was found at a quarter past seven on Thursday evening in the private viewing room, struck on the head by the marble base of a small sculpture. The gallery had closed at six and the viewing room was reserved for staff. Inspector Haldane was called in and spent the next day interviewing the people who had been in or near the building.

Priya, the registrar, was among those interviewed. Priya was due to take a holiday the following week and had spent days handing work over. A rumour that Priya had been arguing loudly in the car park the day before turned out to be about a disputed parking space and nothing more. Priya could not have lifted the marble base; a shoulder injury had kept Priya off any heavy work since spring. Priya had left the building at 6:10 and was photographed at the train station at 6:25 by the station's camera. Priya had learned that Selin was about to report them to the insurers over a painting that had gone missing from storage in Priya's care. The intern had been sent twice to the post office for a courier slip that was never needed.

A school group had left a scatter of crayons on the floor of the entrance hall, and the cleaner had complained about it. The gallery's cafe had run out of oat milk that week, which had put several people in a bad mood. A leak from the roof had forced the staff to move two paintings out of the east wing that afternoon.

Sofia, the head of security, was among those interviewed. Sofia had recently taken up long-distance running and talked about little else at lunch. Sofia owed Selin a large sum for a consignment that had never sold, and Selin had threatened legal action. Sofia had been issued the only spare key to the viewing room that month. Sofia signed out of the staff log at 7:20, five minutes after the estimated time of death, though the receptionist remembered Sofia arriving much earlier. The intern had been sent twice to the post office for a courier slip that was never needed.

Jonas, the gallery's accountant, was among those interviewed. Jonas had been with the organisation for 15 years and was generally regarded as reliable, if a little reserved. Several colleagues thought Jonas had behaved oddly afterwards, but it emerged that Jonas had simply been shaken by the news. Jonas had been told in writing that their contract would not be renewed, and had begged Selin to reconsider in front of several witnesses. Jonas was on a recorded video call with a client abroad throughout the evening, and the call log confirmed it. Jonas had a key to the staff-only viewing room and had been shown how to move the heavy sculptures without help. The gallery's cafe had run out of oat milk that week, which had put several people in a bad mood.

Mei, a visiting art dealer, was among those interviewed. Mei had moved to the area 14 years earlier and was still considered a newcomer by some. Mei was seen by a witness carrying a bag out of the building, which proved to contain only a pair of muddy boots. Mei could not account for a half-hour around the time of the death; the only person who could vouch for Mei was out of the country. Mei had never been issued a key to the viewing room and the door could only be opened from inside by staff. Mei owed Selin a large sum for a consignment that had never sold, and Selin had threatened legal action. The gallery's cafe had run out of oat milk that week, which had put several people in a bad mood.

Inspector Haldane put the notes in order and began to draft a report.
