WORLDWIDE JOURNEY COMPREHENSIVE COVER
Issued by TravSure Mutual


1. DEFINITIONS AND GENERAL TERMS
  1.1 If you are dissatisfied with any aspect of the service, please write to our complaints department at the address on your certificate. We will acknowledge receipt within five working days and provide a final response as soon as our review is complete.
  1.2 Only the traveller named on the certificate may submit a reimbursement request. A request may be made by a legal representative if the traveller is unable to act on their own behalf, provided proof of authority is supplied.
  1.3 To contact TravSure Mutual, write to our correspondence address shown on the certificate or call the telephone number listed in your policy documents. Our customer service team is available during standard business hours in the country of purchase.

2. COVERAGE AND LIMITS
  2.1 The scheme covers the following categories:
  - Trip Cancellation: Covers non-refundable prepaid travel expenses if the trip is cancelled due to sudden illness, injury, or a family emergency. Per-event limit: €400.
  - Medical Expenses: Covers urgent medical treatment, hospital stays, and emergency evacuation during the trip. Per-event limit: €1,000.
  - Lost or Delayed Baggage: Covers the cost of replacing essential items if checked luggage is lost or delayed beyond a reasonable period. Per-event limit: €2,500.
  - Travel Delay: Covers reasonable additional accommodation and meal costs when a common carrier delay disrupts the journey. Per-event limit: €2,000.
  2.2 The per-event limit is applied to the loss first; the deductible of €150 is then subtracted from the capped amount.
  2.3 The traveller bears no co-payment.
  2.4 Total payments in one policy year may not exceed €12,000; amounts already paid in the year reduce what remains.

3. EXCLUSIONS
  3.1 No coverage applies for any medical expense arising from a condition for which the traveller received medical advice or treatment within the period before the policy start date.
  3.2 No reimbursement will be made for injury or loss resulting from the traveller's wilful exposure to unnecessary risk or from participating in an activity banned by this policy.
  3.3 This policy does not cover any loss that occurs while the traveller is in a country or region for which the traveller did not obtain the required travel documents.
  3.4 No benefit is payable for any event directly caused by an act of war, invasion, or a declared terrorist incident as defined by the relevant national authority.

4. CONDITIONS
  4.1 Nothing is payable for a loss occurring fewer than 7 days after the inception date.
  4.2 A reimbursement request must be notified within 14 days after the loss date; later notification is not accepted.
  4.3 Every reimbursement request must be accompanied by the police report.

5. ASSESSMENT PROCEDURE
  Each reimbursement request is assessed in this order and the first applicable step decides it: (a) waiting period (4.1), (b) notification deadline (4.2), (c) exclusions (Section 3; the lowest-numbered applicable exclusion is named), (d) documentation (4.3: the reimbursement request is held, not denied), (e) amount (Section 2), (f) any amount above €1,200 requires senior-adjuster sign-off before payment.

6. PRECEDENCE
  If any other part of these terms conflicts with Section 3 or Section 5, Sections 3 and 5 prevail.
  In this document, 'traveller' means the person named on the certificate of insurance. 'Trip' means the journey booked and paid for before the policy start date. 'Common carrier' means any licensed public transport provider.

7. ADMINISTRATION
  7.1 TravSure Mutual will process all personal data in accordance with applicable data protection law. Information provided in a reimbursement request will be used solely to assess that request and will not be shared with third parties outside of this purpose without the traveller's consent.
  7.2 If any part of this policy is found to be unenforceable, the remainder shall continue in full force and effect. This severability clause ensures that a single invalid provision does not invalidate the entire agreement.

Titre : Impact d'un programme de lecture assistée sur les compétences en littératie

Résumé : Cette étude examine l'effet d'un programme de lecture assistée par tablette sur les compétences en lecture des élèves de 3e année. Un échantillon de 45 élèves a participé à une intervention de 4 semaines (20 minutes par jour, 5 jours par semaine). Les résultats pré- et post-intervention ont été mesurés à l'aide d'un test standardisé de compréhension de texte (échelle 0-100).

Résultats : Le score moyen pré-test était de 58,4 (ET = 9,2). À la fin de la période de 4 semaines, le score moyen post-test était de 61,7 (ET = 8,8), soit une amélioration de 3,3 points (t = 2,01, p = 0,051). Aucun effet significatif n'a été observé sur la fluence de lecture ni sur le vocabulaire réceptif. Les enseignants ont rapporté une satisfaction générale à l'égard du programme, bien que certains aient noté des difficultés techniques occasionnelles avec les appareils.

Limitations : Cette étude comporte plusieurs limites, notamment la petite taille de l'échantillon, l'absence de groupe témoin, et la courte durée de l'intervention. Ces facteurs limitent la généralisation des résultats. Des recherches futures devraient inclure un suivi à long terme et des mesures comportementales complémentaires.

semántica: Los eventos se procesan estrictamente en el orden indicado. Tras un evento, las reglas que coinciden se activan en orden ascendente de número de regla y cada acción se aplica de inmediato.
Una regla con condición solo se activa si la condición se cumple en ese momento; una regla marcada como «única» solo se activa la primera vez que coinciden su disparador y su condición.

Una orden directa del usuario fija el dispositivo y lo pone en retención manual. Las acciones de automatización sobre un dispositivo retenido se omiten hasta el siguiente evento de «modo», que libera todas las retenciones antes de que se activen sus reglas. Las órdenes no activan reglas por sí mismas.
Una cerradura no puede ponerse en «locked» mientras el sensor de su puerta indique «open»: la acción se ignora (la cerradura conserva su valor y no hay cambio). Desbloquear siempre es posible.
Las consignas del termostato (dispositivos heat) se limitan al rango 18-25: un valor mayor o menor se guarda como el límite más cercano.

Cuando un dispositivo cambia realmente de valor (causado por una orden del usuario o por una regla; no hay cambio si ya tenía ese valor), las reglas con disparador «el dispositivo pasa a valor» se ponen en cola y se activan después de las reglas propias del evento actual, en el orden en que ocurrieron los cambios.

state.policy:
Travel and Expense Policy. This policy governs reimbursement of business-trip expenses for employees. Amounts are in euros.
1. Definitions. A "business trip" is a trip with at least one overnight stay away from the employee's home city that has been approved in advance. A "travel day" is any calendar day from the day of departure to the day of return, both included. "Grade" is the employee's grade from 1 to 4 as shown on the claim. City class A, B or C is assigned to the destination in Annex 1.
2. Hotel. The hotel is reimbursed per night up to the cap for the city class and grade (euros per night): class A: 170 (grades 1-2) / 190 (grades 3-4); class B: 120 (grades 1-2) / 135 (grades 3-4); class C: 85 (grades 1-2) / 105 (grades 3-4). Amounts above the cap are not reimbursed; the cap applies to every night.
3. Meals. Meals are reimbursed as a flat allowance of 48 euros per travel day. On the first and the last travel day the allowance is 60 % of that amount. For each meal that was provided free of charge (for example at a conference), the allowance of that travel day is reduced by 20 % of the full daily amount for breakfast and 30 % for lunch or dinner; the allowance of a day never falls below zero. No receipts are needed for the allowance.
4. Flights. Flights are reimbursed at the economy fare. Business class is reimbursed in full only if the flight lasts more than 7 hours and the employee is grade 4 or higher; otherwise the reimbursement is limited to the economy fare that the claim states for the same flight.
5. Local transport. Public transport and taxis at the destination are reimbursed up to 15 euros per travel day in total. Items of more than 20 euros need an original receipt. Items of up to 20 euros without a receipt are reimbursed only if those items together do not exceed 60 euros; otherwise none of them is reimbursed.
6. Excluded items. Alcoholic drinks, minibar, personal entertainment and leisure, spa and fitness, parking fines and any other fines are never reimbursed, even if they appear on a hotel invoice.
7. Private car. If the employee uses a private car, mileage is reimbursed at 0.30 euros per kilometre. This clause does not apply to taxis or rented cars.
8. Late claims. A claim must be submitted within 45 days after the day of return. If it is submitted later but within 75 days, the total reimbursable amount is reduced by 15 %. After 75 days the claim is rejected.
9. Approval. The approver is determined by the total reimbursable amount after all deductions: up to and including 500 euros the line manager approves; above that and up to and including 1500 euros the department head approves; above 1500 euros the finance director approves. A rejected claim needs no approval.
10. Records. Claims and receipts are kept for ten years. Personal data on receipts is processed under the company data protection notice.
Additional provisions (these do not change the numbered clauses above):
- Advance payments. Employees may request an advance of up to 70 % of the expected hotel and travel costs, at the earliest ten days before departure. Advances are settled against the claim and do not change the rules for reimbursement.
- Spouses and guests. Costs for accompanying persons are never reimbursed, including their share of a shared room or meal.
- Loyalty programmes. Points, miles and bonus credits earned on business trips may be kept by the employee. They may not be used to upgrade a booking that the company pays for.
- Disputes. If an employee disagrees with a decision on a claim, a written objection can be sent to the finance department within 14 days of the decision.
Annex 1. City classes: A = capital and financial centres; B = other cities above 250,000 inhabitants; C = all other places.

state.story:
Hello, Sam,

The teaching lab was quiet when I arrived, except for the ventilation fan and the alarm panel chirping by the storeroom. Professor Adrian Vale was on the floor beside the open cabinet, conscious but badly hurt. Someone had struck him and taken the university’s brass calibration standard, a small instrument used in the lab’s demonstrations. The storeroom door had not been forced. Vale was taken for treatment, and I asked everyone who had been in the building to stay available while I worked out what had happened.

The room’s access log showed no useful record of the storeroom door opening. Its lock could be released with a key, or with the master code. The department kept just one master code, normally secured in an office drawer. I checked the drawer and found it shut, with no sign of damage. A borrowing sheet and messages from the staff showed that three people had taken the code for legitimate work the day before: Marcus Oyelaran, Dana Whitlock, and Kofi Mensah. None reported returning it before the incident. That established who could have known the code, but it did not place anyone at the storeroom.

Greta Vogel had another route through the lock. The storeroom key had been issued to her for the lab’s equipment checks, and the key register showed it was still assigned to her. When I asked about her relationship with Vale, she did not deny that things had turned sour. Last month, during a public lab meeting, Vale had embarrassed her in front of the teaching staff over a mistake in a demonstration. Two people who attended remembered the exchange and said Greta had looked shaken afterward. She told me she had been angry, but said the argument was over.

A technician’s account put Greta in the corridor near the storeroom during the critical half hour. The technician had gone back to fetch a notebook and saw Greta there by herself. The account did not establish what she was doing, and the technician had not seen anyone enter or leave the storeroom. Greta said she was checking equipment. Her explanation was possible, but the witness could not confirm it.

Marcus Oyelaran had also been embarrassed by Vale last month. A student and a lab assistant both recalled Vale criticizing Marcus in public after a demonstration went wrong. Marcus said the incident had bothered him, though he had since made peace with it. His name was on the borrowing sheet for the master code, but the building’s departure record and a call he made from outside the campus showed that he had left before the critical half hour began. He could not have been in the lab during the attack, even if he had known how to open the storeroom.

Dana Whitlock’s connection to Vale was different. They had a business arrangement, and the paperwork showed that Dana stood to inherit Vale’s share of that business. Dana had borrowed the master code the day before, according to the same sheet. But the front desk attendant remembered Dana leaving, and the building record placed Dana outside before the critical half hour began. Dana told me the code had been needed for routine work and denied going back inside.

Kofi Mensah had also borrowed the master code the day before. He did not have the same history of conflict with Vale: several people described them as being on excellent terms, and I found a record showing that Kofi had lent Vale money. Kofi said they had stayed friends despite the debt. No one could account for Kofi’s whereabouts during the critical half hour. He said he had been moving between work areas, but nobody could vouch for that account, and no reliable record put him elsewhere.

There were distractions. A cabinet elsewhere in the lab had been left open, but its contents were intact. Someone had also spilled coffee near the corridor, though the spill was dry and unrelated to the assault. Neither detail changed the access records or the accounts I had collected. Vale was harmed, the calibration standard was gone, and the investigation still depended on matching the evidence about access, personal stakes, and whereabouts.

state.story:
Bellwether House was quiet except for the rasp of sandpaper and the hollow knocks of cabinet doors being fitted when the trouble began. The kitchen renovation had forced the household to move its dishes and keepsakes into a locked storeroom off the service passage. Inside, on a padded shelf, sat a silver serving tray the victim had been supervising the restoration of. The victim was found injured beside the kitchen island; the tray was missing. The injury was serious enough to require care, but the victim survived and could not give the investigator a reliable account of what had happened.

The investigator arrived while the work crew was still clearing dust from the counters. Nothing in the kitchen suggested a struggle beyond a chair lying on its side and a smear on the island’s edge. The storeroom door showed no damage. Its electronic lock accepted a master code, and the household’s records described that code as the only master code. A separate key also opened the storeroom. The investigator warned everyone not to treat a clean lock as proof that nobody had entered; the door had been used repeatedly during the renovation.

Priya Raman spoke with the investigator near the pantry. Several people had heard the victim publicly humiliate Priya Raman last month, during a discussion about the renovation. Priya Raman did not deny that the exchange had been painful, though they said the argument should not be mistaken for proof of anything. A contractor recalled hearing raised voices, but could not say what followed. The code log showed that Priya Raman had borrowed the only master code the day before. The log recorded its return, but it did not establish who knew or used the code afterward. When the investigator asked about the critical half hour, nobody could vouch for Priya Raman’s whereabouts throughout that interval.

Samir Haddad had been helping sort kitchen fittings. Two household members told the investigator that Samir Haddad had no quarrel with the victim and had recently been praised by them for careful work. The same code log showed that Samir Haddad had borrowed the only master code the day before. A delivery worker, interviewed separately, said Samir Haddad was alone near the scene during the critical half hour. The worker had not seen anyone enter the storeroom and could not say how long Samir Haddad remained there. The investigator wrote down both the limits of the observation and what it did establish.

Dana Whitlock’s name appeared on the access record too, but an earlier entry showed that Dana Whitlock had handed back their code a week earlier. The household had no record of a later loan. A camera at another site showed Dana Whitlock there throughout the critical half hour; its continuous view included the entrance and the work area. In conversation, two people described Dana Whitlock as having no quarrel with the victim and as someone the victim had recently praised. The investigator checked those accounts against the renovation notes. Neither suggested a dispute.

Aiko Tanaka had been working with the household’s stored fittings and had a key to the locked storeroom where the silver serving tray was kept. Aiko Tanaka told the investigator that the tray had been placed on its padded shelf before the incident. The household inventory confirmed its usual location, though no one had made a fresh check immediately before the victim was found. Aiko Tanaka had gained nothing from the victim’s absence, according to the household’s account of the tray and the planned work. A neighbor had seen Aiko Tanaka alone near the scene during the critical half hour. The neighbor could not see inside the storeroom.

The investigator also examined two distractions. A damp mark beside the sink came from a leaking fitting the crew had already been monitoring; it did not lead toward the storeroom. A cabinet hinge had gone missing earlier in the renovation and was later found beneath a folded drop cloth. Neither detail connected anyone to the injury or the missing tray. The investigator recorded them because small, ordinary messes can acquire an unwarranted meaning after a crime, especially in a house full of tools and half-finished work.

Before leaving, the investigator compared the access record, the camera footage, and each witness’s account, noting where a statement was direct and where it was only an inference. The renovation had left the kitchen exposed and busy, but the relevant accounts concerned the same critical half hour and the same locked room. The investigator asked the household to keep the remaining records intact while the inquiry continued.

The company employed 46 people at year-end, up from 42 the previous year, and operated from a 28,000-square-foot facility. Despite higher sales, operating costs rose as well. The cost of steel and electronic components increased, and the company recorded $95,000 in expedited-shipping expenses after a supplier delay affected several spring orders. Cedar Vale reported a year-end operating profit of $610,000, compared with $575,000 the year before. semantics: Events are processed strictly in the listed order. After an event, the rules that match it fire in ascending rule number, and each action is applied immediately.
A rule with a condition fires only if the condition holds at that moment; a rule marked "once" fires only the first time its trigger and condition match.

A direct user command sets the device and puts it on manual hold. Automation actions on a held device are skipped until the next "mode" event, which releases all holds before its rules fire. Commands do not trigger rules by themselves.
A lock cannot be set to locked while its door sensor reads open: the action is ignored (the lock keeps its value, and no change happens). Unlocking is always possible.
Thermostat setpoints (heat devices) are limited to the range 17-25: a larger or smaller value is stored as the nearest limit.

When a device actually changes value (caused by a user command or by a rule; no change if it already had that value), rules with trigger "device becomes value" are queued and fire after the current event's own rules, in the order the changes happened.
Value codes: on@N = light on at N % brightness, off, on/off for plugs, locked/unlocked, open/closed for blinds, a number = thermostat setpoint in °C.

documents: D1. Unmatched Pattern Policies: When a shell pattern used as a pathname expression matches no files, the default behavior in many shells is to leave the pattern unchanged as an ordinary argument. Bash offers two options that change this. With nullglob enabled, an unmatched pattern expands to zero words, which can make a command receive no operand at all. With failglob enabled, the shell reports an error and does not run the command. These options affect pathname expansion, not pattern tests in conditional expressions. Choose deliberately when a script must distinguish an empty directory from a filename that literally contains wildcard characters.

D2. Single and Double Quotes: In a POSIX-style shell, single quotes preserve every enclosed character literally, except that a single quote cannot appear inside a single-quoted region. Double quotes also preserve most characters, but still allow parameter expansion, command substitution, and arithmetic expansion. A backslash inside double quotes is special only before a dollar sign, backtick, double quote, backslash, or newline. These forms are useful for different goals: single quotes protect text completely, while double quotes protect text while allowing selected values to be inserted. Quotes group shell syntax; they are removed before the resulting argument is passed to a command.

D3. Bracket Expressions in Patterns: A bracket expression in a shell pathname pattern matches one character from a specified set or range. For example, a pattern can select names whose next character is one of several listed letters, and a leading exclamation mark inside the brackets negates the set in Bash. The expression matches a single character position, not an arbitrary-length substring. A hyphen can indicate a range, but its interpretation can depend on locale; spelling out individual characters avoids some surprises. Bracket expressions are active during pathname expansion when the pattern is unquoted. Quoting the brackets makes them ordinary characters instead.

D4. Word Splitting and IFS: After certain expansions, an unquoted result is subject to word splitting. The shell uses the characters in IFS to identify separators; its default value contains space, tab, and newline. Runs of IFS whitespace are generally treated as separators, while other IFS characters have additional boundary behavior. Splitting is not a general rule for every piece of command text: it applies to eligible expansion results, not to literal spaces typed between words. Double-quoting an expansion suppresses this splitting. For data that may contain arbitrary whitespace, relying on this mechanism is usually unsafe; explicit arrays or line-oriented reading are more predictable.

D5. Quoting a Variable Expansion: When a variable expansion is left unquoted, the shell may perform word splitting on its result and then pathname expansion on the resulting words. A value containing spaces can therefore become several command arguments, and wildcard characters in the value can be treated as file-matching patterns. Writing the expansion inside double quotes preserves it as one argument, including when the value is empty. This is the usual safe form when passing a variable as one operand, such as a path or user-supplied string. Quoting the expansion does not prevent the variable's value from being substituted.

D6. Disabling Pathname Expansion: Bash can disable pathname expansion with the set -f option, also called noglob. While this setting is active, wildcard characters produced by an otherwise eligible word are not used to search for matching filenames; they remain literal characters in the argument. This does not disable parameter expansion, command substitution, or word splitting, so it is not equivalent to quoting every expansion. The setting remains in effect for later commands in the shell until reversed with set +f. In a script that changes it temporarily, restore the prior state carefully, especially when code may return early or run inside a function.

D7. Locale and Pattern Result Order: After pathname patterns match directory entries, shells commonly present the resulting names in a sorted order. In Bash, that order is affected by the current locale, especially the setting that controls collation. Consequently, names containing uppercase letters, digits, or accented characters may not appear in the bytewise order a developer expects. Setting LC_ALL=C for a command or script gives a stable byte-oriented ordering in common environments. This sorting behavior applies to the list produced by pathname expansion; it does not reorder arguments that never came from a pattern. Programs needing a specific order should state that requirement rather than assume one.

D8. Arrays Preserve Argument Boundaries: Bash indexed arrays can store multiple values while preserving the boundary between each value. To pass every stored value as a separate argument, expand the array using the at-sign form inside double quotes. This produces one argument per element, including elements containing spaces, and produces no arguments for an empty array. The star form inside double quotes instead joins the elements into one argument, using the first character of IFS as the separator. Unquoted array expansions can expose elements to splitting and pathname expansion. Arrays are therefore a reliable way to construct an argument list incrementally without encoding boundaries in a string.

D9. Leading Dots in Pathname Patterns: In Bash, a pathname pattern beginning with an ordinary wildcard does not normally match a filename whose first character is a dot. Thus a pattern such as an asterisk will usually skip entries like configuration files, even though they are present in the directory. A dot at the start of a filename must be matched explicitly, or the shell option dotglob can be enabled to include such names in wildcard results. The special directory entries dot and dot-dot remain excluded from ordinary wildcard matches. This rule concerns pathname expansion; it does not determine what a command such as ls chooses to display.

D11. Trailing Newlines in Command Substitution: Command substitution runs a command and inserts its standard output into the surrounding shell word. Bash removes all trailing newline characters from that output before insertion, not merely one final newline. Newlines within the output remain, subject to the surrounding quoting and later processing. This behavior makes command substitution convenient for capturing textual results, but it means it cannot preserve an output value whose meaningful ending consists of newline characters. If exact byte preservation matters, use a mechanism designed for that purpose rather than storing the result this way. Any diagnostic text written to standard error is not included in the substituted value.

Una regla con condición solo se activa si la condición se cumple en ese momento; una regla marcada como «única» solo se activa la primera vez que coinciden su disparador y su condición.

The vault is accessed by keycard, and the camera over the door had been switched to maintenance mode for the day. Inspector Okonkwo began by reviewing the keycard log and interviewing the library staff.

The people of interest were Aiko, the head librarian, Wei, the IT administrator, Jonas, the rare-book dealer, and Noah, a donor.

The air-conditioning had been tweaked that week to protect a new acquisition, and everybody complained of the cold. A group of schoolchildren had been taken through the main hall that morning. The cafe had changed its supplier of biscuits, to general disapproval.

state.story:
Ticket: Neighbourhood association budget-room inquiry

The budget meeting had barely reached the argument over the courtyard lights when the chairperson stopped mid-sentence. A crash came from the maintenance room, followed by a shout. The victim was found badly hurt beside a powered cutting tool used for repairs. Someone had moved the tool from its usual rack, and a smear of paint on the doorway made the scene look, at first, like a botched attempt to get in. The investigator arrived while the meeting was still breaking into anxious groups. The victim was taken for treatment; the investigator kept everyone in the hall and began asking who had been where.

The victim had a stake in a small business connected to the association’s property work. The business mattered because its ownership arrangements had become a subject of quiet conversation. Several people at the meeting stood to inherit the victim’s share. The investigator did not let the rumour about money settle the matter: inheritance could explain a reason to wish harm, but it could not place anyone in the maintenance room.

Lucía Ferreira had been helping assemble the budget papers. She said she and the victim had got on without friction, and the victim had praised her work recently in front of other volunteers. Nothing in the messages the investigator reviewed suggested a dispute between them. The maintenance crew confirmed that Lucía had never been taught to use the cutting tool. She also told the investigator she had gone home before the critical half hour began; the building’s departure log and a neighbour who saw her leave supported that account.

Kofi Mensah had been at the meeting earlier, carrying a folder of receipts. He described the victim as a friend, and several people confirmed that the two had been on very good terms. Kofi had lent the victim money, not demanded it back. The investigator checked the access records after Kofi mentioned that he had returned his code a week earlier. The return was logged, and Kofi had left the building before the critical half hour began. One volunteer recalled seeing him pause by the side entrance, but the door had jammed and he was only helping hold it open while someone fetched the caretaker. That detail made for tense talk, but changed nothing in the records.

Samir Haddad was easier to place. He had a financial interest in what happened to the victim’s business share, and the business documents supported the claim that he would inherit it. He was also among the people trained to handle the powered tool; the maintenance log listed his instruction. But during the critical half hour, Samir was giving a presentation to a room of colleagues. The investigator spoke with those in attendance and checked the meeting-room recording. A draft budget slide had gone missing from his presentation folder, which prompted an unnecessary argument, but it had no bearing on his whereabouts.

Priya Raman’s name appeared in the same business papers. Like Samir, Priya stood to inherit the victim’s share, and the maintenance log showed that Priya had been trained to use the tool. Priya said they had spent the relevant stretch in the building, moving between the hall and the corridor outside the maintenance room. The investigator checked the sign-in notes, the door records, and the statements gathered from people still at the meeting. None could vouch for Priya’s location during the critical half hour. Priya’s sleeve had a streak of blue paint, but the paint matched the fresh marks left on the budget-board frame, not the smear at the doorway. It was a small, distracting coincidence, and no more.

Owen Pritchard also had a stake in the business and would inherit the victim’s share. He had the same tool qualification noted in the maintenance log. The investigator found no dispute between Owen and the victim that evening, but the inheritance remained a possible reason for hostility. The camera at another site showed Owen there throughout the critical half hour. The footage was continuous, and the site supervisor confirmed the recording had not been interrupted.

By the time the investigator finished, the room had gone quiet except for the hum of the projector. The budget papers were still spread across the table, the tool remained sealed away, and the victim was alive but seriously harmed. The investigator asked for the notes to be kept separate: what the records established, what people had heard, and what was only speculation. Then the investigator turned to the association’s legal adviser and asked for a decision based on the full account, not the loudest accusation.

Value codes: on@N = light on at N % brightness, off, on/off for plugs, locked/unlocked, open/closed for blinds, a number = thermostat setpoint in °C.

state.story:
Reference: Kitchen renovation incident file.

The kitchen had been opened down to its plaster and joists, and the household had learned to treat every locked door as a temporary fixture. The narrow storeroom off the back passage held the renovation’s heavy demolition hammer, along with boxes of salvaged fittings. During the work, the victim was found badly injured beside the storeroom threshold. The hammer was recovered nearby. The investigator recorded the injury as an assault and asked the household and crew to account for what they had seen, without assuming that the disorder of a building site explained anything.

The first account came from the homeowner, who said the victim had been supervising the kitchen work and was expected to approve the next stage. Owen Pritchard had hoped to receive a promotion connected with that work, but the victim had been selected instead. Owen’s disappointment had not been a secret: a household member recalled a tense conversation about the decision, though could not say whether it had gone beyond frustration. The investigator treated that exchange cautiously. A grievance could matter, but by itself it proved little.

The storeroom lock had not been forced. The owner’s key record showed that Owen Pritchard had a key for it. The hammer had been kept inside, and several people knew where it belonged. The investigator noted the distinction between knowing the location and being able to open the room. A scuffed strip of protective floor covering ran from the passage toward the kitchen, but the crew said such marks were common during renovation; it offered no reliable account of who had crossed it.

Kofi Mensah had no personal gain to expect from the victim’s absence, according to the people interviewed. Their accounts described no dispute over money, work, or household decisions. Kofi had, however, received training in the safe handling of the demolition hammer. That training was part of the practical work, and the investigator confirmed it from the crew’s records. Kofi could not account for their whereabouts during the critical half hour: nobody came forward to say they had been with Kofi, and the available records did not settle the point.

Samir Haddad’s circumstances looked different in some respects. The victim and Samir had been on excellent terms, and Samir had lent the victim money. The investigator checked whether the loan had become a source of friction; the statements gathered gave no indication of that, and the relationship was described as warm. Samir, like Kofi, had been trained to handle the demolition hammer. Yet the site’s camera record placed Samir at another location for the whole critical half hour. The investigator verified that the recording covered the relevant period, while noting that a camera can establish where a person appeared to be, not what they were thinking.

Greta Vogel was also described as being on excellent terms with the victim, and Greta had lent the victim money. Those who spoke to the investigator said the loan had not spoiled their friendship. Greta had neither access to the storeroom nor a key for its lock. The camera record also showed Greta at another location throughout the critical half hour. Greta had not received training in handling the demolition hammer, either, though the investigator did not treat that detail as a substitute for checking the lock and the recording.

A delivery docket left on the counter bore no connection to the assault, and a missing packet of cabinet screws turned up later beneath a folded drop cloth. Both had briefly distracted the household, but neither altered the evidence about the storeroom, the hammer, or the accounts of the people under review. The investigator kept the statements separate from the physical observations and left a note that the renovation’s clutter made casual sightings especially unreliable.

By the time the kitchen was sealed for the evening, the file contained the key record, the training records, the camera account, and the separate statements about the victim’s relationships and the promotion decision. None of those entries, taken alone, settled the matter. The investigator set them beside the circumstances of the assault and asked the household to consider who could have carried it out.

ticket.subject: Interpreting counterfactual from randomized drug trial data for tomorrow's seminar
ticket.body: We're preparing a case study on the Novartis-2023 antibiotic trial for our graduate seminar. Students will see this summary: every enrolled patient has exactly one immutable response profile—16% are "responders" who would recover only if given the antibiotic, 32% are "non-responders" who would not recover regardless, and 52% are "always-recover" patients who would recover whether or not they received the antibiotic. Treatment assignment was fully randomized, with no connection to a patient's underlying profile. The puzzle case: we observe a patient who was randomized to the placebo arm and did not recover. The students must reason about what would have happened to this same individual had they instead been randomized to receive the antibiotic. I want to be careful here—there's a subtlety about whether we're asking for a population probability or something individual, and I know the randomization matters for the inference. Could you confirm the exact proposition I should pose?
